| [LIT-156](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-156.md) v4 | An Emerging Dilemma for Reciprocal Causation | Hazelwood (2023), DOI-10.1017/psa.2023.124. Hazelwood defines RC as "the process of natural selection is both a cause and effect of processes such as niche construction" and EC as "natural selection is an emergent causal process". He argues they are incompatible. Emergence here is Wilson's synchronic dependence plus autonomy, cashed out as Pence's composition. If EC holds, niche construction partly composes selection, so the two fail Woodward's independent-fixability condition and cannot stand in a causal relation. If EC fails, selection is either non-causal (statisticalism) or individual-level, which is incoherent because relative fitness needs a population (Millstein, Sober). EES proponents should drop RC but can keep niche construction as a genuine cause of the evolutionary *product*. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-137.md)); worth reading as a tight, well-sourced argument that brings the reciprocal-causation debate into the composition, exclusion and interventionism literature. | [LIT-157](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-157.md) v3 | Reproducees, reproducers, and Darwinian individuals | Bourrat (2025), DOI-10.1007/s11229-024-04880-w. Bourrat builds a nested vocabulary. A reproducee is a B that comes after A, is caused by A, and is of A's relevant class. A reproducer is a reproducee with reproductive autonomy, meaning it can reproduce across a range of backgrounds. A Darwinian individual is a reproducer with high reproductive causal control, meaning heredity survives as the parent's description is made finer. On that vocabulary, genes of multicellular organisms are, like hearts, mere reproducees, but with high control. Material overlap is necessary for reproducers, which are whole life cycles, and unnecessary for reproducees, so Griesemer and Godfrey-Smith partly talk past each other. Both quantities get an information-theoretic recipe (conditional MI after Bertschinger et al. 2008 for autonomy; interventional MI across grains, Griffiths et al.'s INF, for control), and neither is computed. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-100](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-100.md)); worth reading as the clearest statement of the reproduced/reproducing distinction and a tidy, well-scoped settlement of the material-overlap dispute. Its value is conceptual. Its two measures are recipes that are never computed, and the autonomy recipe does not match its own verbal definition. |

Lloyd's own four-question anatomy of "unit of selection": interactor, reproducer (formerly replicator), manifestor of adaptation, and beneficiary. She combines it with a split between two multilevel schools, Wrightian "Evolutionary Change" and Fisherian "Adaptationist/KS". She uses the two to argue for a verdict, not merely to map the debates. The verdict is that most rejections of group, species and holobiont selection come from demanding that an interactor also be a manifestor of *engineering* adaptation. The entry reports no new results of its own. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-184](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-184.md)); worth reading as the authoritative statement of the interactor / reproducer / manifestor / beneficiary distinction and as a dense map of the units-of-selection literature to 2023. | [LIT-169](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-169.md) v2 | Defining the niche for niche construction: evolutionary and ecological niches | Trappes (2021), DOI-10.1007/s10539-021-09805-2. Trappes compares NCT's evolutionary niche with the ecological niche. The evolutionary niche is the sum of selection pressures on a population (Odling-Smee, Laland & Feldman 2003), read "externally" as the environmental factors that produce fitness differences. The ecological niche is the conditions that permit continued existence; for a population, mean absolute fitness ≥ 1. Even at their closest, against the realized population niche, the two differ in extension. Habitat degradation is in the evolutionary niche but not the ecological one, and commensalism and non-limiting resources are in the ecological niche but not the evolutionary one. So NCT's niche is not the "simple translation" of Hutchinson's niche its proponents claim, and the evolutionary significance of niche construction must be shown case by case rather than following from the definition. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-155](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-155.md)); worth reading as a short, clean conceptual analysis that turns "persistence versus fitness differences" into a precise wedge between two fields' uses of "niche"; its empirical cases are admittedly thin (the CO2 case is offered as "possible"), and it analyses only the 2003 book's niche concept. |

Worrall argues that the EBM evidence hierarchy has no sound general rationale for giving randomisation extra epistemic weight, even though it lets high-quality RCTs "trump any number of observational studies". He examines five standard arguments. Four fail: (a) Fisher's significance-test logic, (b) control of unknown confounders, (d) that observational studies "exaggerate" effects, and (e) probabilistic causality. The fifth, (c) selection bias, is a "cast-iron argument", but it supports only taking allocation out of the clinicians' hands, and randomisation is one way to do that. What matters is balance on plausible confounders, a placebo or active control and blinding. Whether balance comes from randomising or from matching "seems epistemically unimportant", and historically controlled trials can give strong evidence for large effects. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-126.md)); worth reading as the fullest single statement of the philosophical case against the special epistemic standing of randomisation. The paper sets out an idealized three-stage sequence of interaction types, which it calls a "first and rough sketch" (§1). Stage 1 is coordination in *collections* (pairwise, "aggregative" interactions of co-located individuals). Stage 2 is cooperation in *conexuses* (a connected web of binary interactions whose benefits can still be counted per member). Stage 3 is collaboration in *communities*: heterogeneous multi-way interactions around a shared goal, in which generatively entrenched "core" interactions give organizational closure. Table 1 puts the transition to a new level of individuality between stages 2 and 3 only. The paper asserts, rather than argues, that this describes evolutionary transitions non-circularly and that individuality is a special case of collectivity. Its one argued conclusion is hedged: community-level inheritance "seem[s] likely to evolve in tandem" with community-level individuality (§3). | Proposed — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-173](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-173.md)); a short programmatic sketch, and the authors call it one. Its headline claims (non-circularity; individuality as a special case of collectivity) appear only in the abstract. Two things would settle it: the model of community "reliability" and endogenization the authors promise in §2 ("We hope to explore such models in future work"), or an application of the 3Cs to a worked case, such as the companion Neolithic paper (LIT-1935, registered unread), that separates collection, conexus and community by measurable criteria. Bennett states Landauer's principle as a consequence of the Second Law. A logically irreversible step, meaning erasure or a *merge of control flow*, must export at least the lost entropy (k ln 2 per bit) to non-information-bearing degrees of freedom. That export need not take the form of heat (p. 1). Logically reversible operations, including copying onto a blank register and measurement, have no minimum cost. He calls "an intrinsic cost of order kT for every elementary act of information processing" a 20th-century "misconception" (pp. 5–6). A one-locus model in which an individual's genotype affects relatives' fitness. Weighting each effect by Wright's coefficient of relationship r gives "inclusive fitness", which tends to be maximized as classical fitness is. It proves that mean inclusive fitness increases only for genes whose total effect on others is non-negative (giving traits); for harming traits it shows only that selection points uphill. There is no Hawk–Dove game and no ownership asymmetry here. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-404](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-404.md)); worth reading as the paper that introduced the evolutionarily stable strategy and showed that "limited war" in animal contests can be favoured by individual selection. It is not the source of the Hawk–Dove game or of owner–intruder conventions, though morality-as-cooperation cites it for both: its strategies are Mouse, Hawk, Bully, Retaliator and Prober-Retaliator, its contestants are symmetric, and its "Retaliator is an ESS" ties with Mouse, so it fails the paper's own second ESS condition. What it does ground for MAC's contest domains is restraint backed by retaliation, and, informally, retreat before a visibly superior opponent and honest signals of formidability. |
| [LIT-506](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-506.md) v2 | The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour. II | Hamilton (1964), J. Theor. Biol. 7:17–52. Part I's model is generalized, "unrigorously", into two principles: an animal values a neighbour's fitness against its own by their relationship, and its social discriminations evolve to make relationship more determinate. They are applied to alarm calls, clones and colonies, the haplodiploid hypothesis for hymenopteran sociality, multiple mating, fights between relatives, sibling competition and seed provisioning. Evidence is anecdotal, and the author reports where it runs against him. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-410](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-410.md)); worth reading as the place inclusive fitness is turned into two general principles (valuing neighbours by relatedness; evolving discrimination that makes relatedness determinate) and tried on warning behaviour, social insects, clones, fights and parental care. The principles are offered as an "unrigorous" generalization of Part I, and the evidence is anecdotal and, by the author's account, partly contrary. Its §6 on fights is the one place in Hamilton's pair that touches contests: relatives should fight less, a kin-weighted version of the restraint Maynard Smith and Price derived without kinship. |
| [LIT-508](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-508.md) | A mutualistic approach to morality: The evolution of fairness by partner choice | Baumard, André & Sperber (2013), DOI-10.1017/S0140525X11002202. When individuals can choose partners and have equal outside options, a split that gives one side less than it could get elsewhere is not stable, so partner choice selects for sharing the gains of cooperation in proportion to contribution. Competition to be chosen then favours a genuine, non-instrumental sense of fairness. Economic-game results (entitlement effects, merit-based division, need-based mutual aid, proportionate punishment) are reinterpreted as fairness, not altruism. Morality is defined as fairness; kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-407](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-407.md)), with all 28 open peer commentaries and the authors' Response; worth reading as the strongest single-mechanism cooperative theory of morality and as the parent of moral disciplining ([LIT-101](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-101.md)). It is a cooperation theory that cuts the other way from morality-as-cooperation: partner choice selects one moral sense, fairness, and kin care and group loyalty are not intrinsically moral. Its evidence is a reinterpretation of others' economic-game results, and its central formal claim is cited from the authors' separate model. The commentaries (Graham, Ramlakhan & Brook, Machery & Stich, Sachdeva et al., Atran) press the purity, harm and scope objections, and the Response answers them two ways because the authors disagree among themselves. |
| [LIT-510](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-510.md) | The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism | Trivers (1971), DOI-10.1086/406755. Altruism between non-relatives can be selected if acts cost the giver less than they benefit the recipient, the same partners meet repeatedly and symmetrically, and altruists stop helping those who fail to reciprocate. Cleaner-fish hosts fit; bird alarm calls are explained instead by self-interest. In humans, friendship, moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt, suspicion and their sham versions are proposed as adaptations that regulate exchange, and rules of conduct as a multiparty extension. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-402](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-402.md)); worth reading as the source of reciprocal altruism and, for this record above all, of the first adaptive account of moral emotions: moralistic aggression, gratitude, sympathy, guilt and the detection of sham versions of each, with "norms of reciprocal conduct" as a later step. The formal part is slight (a verbal model and Hamilton's communicated Prisoner's Dilemma sketch); the human psychology is hypothesis supported by the social-psychology literature of the 1960s. It grounds the exchange domain of morality-as-cooperation and gives that domain its emotions. |
| [LIT-514](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-514.md) v3 | Moral Origins: The Evolution of Virtue, Altruism, and Shame | Boehm (2012), Basic Books. By the publisher's account, the moral sense is "a sophisticated defense mechanism": group punishment of bullies, thieves, free riders and psychopaths over six million years made social selection favour altruists and bred conscience, virtue and shame. The chapter list adds a "selection-by-reputation hypothesis" and its test. Unread: filed from the description and chapter list. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. The book is lending-only at the Internet Archive (item moraloriginsevol0000boeh) and sold by Basic Books. What it argues is known here only from the publisher's description, labelled as such. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-515](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-515.md) | Statistical physics of self-replication | England (2012; J. Chem. Phys. 2013), arXiv:1209.1179. For a system in a heat bath obeying detailed balance, a transition between coarse-grained ensembles I → II obeys β⟨ΔQ⟩ + ln π(II→I) + ΔS_int ≥ 0 (Eq. 6), a second law stated for macrostates. Applied to self-replication, the reverse probability is small when the copy is durable and made fast, so the heat released per copy is bounded below by about 2n ln(n τ_decay/τ_div) − ΔS_int (Eq. 8). The author's estimates put E. coli within a factor of three of this bound and a self-replicating RNA near it. The "self" in self-replication is an observer's classification of microstates, not a physical given. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-419](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-419.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published J. Chem. Phys. text was not reached. Worth reading as the founding paper of the "dissipation-driven" programme and as a clean worked use of a macrostate fluctuation relation: the heat a replicator must release is bounded below by how fast it copies and how durable the copy is, not by the copying itself. The general bound (Eq. 6) is a coarse-grained second law and is sound; the numbers for E. coli and RNA rest on an argued, not derived, upper bound on the reverse probability (Eq. 7). It draws no line between living and non-living replicators, and says so: "self" is a classification an observer supplies. |
| [LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md) | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine (1977), Nobel Lecture, reprinted in Science 201:777 (1978). Near equilibrium the second-order excess entropy δ²S is a Lyapounov function, so fluctuations die out, and in the "strictly" linear regime the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium the sign of the excess entropy production ΣδJδX is no longer fixed. Given autocatalytic steps (necessary, not sufficient) the thermodynamic branch can go unstable, and fluctuations are amplified into "dissipative structures": Bénard convection, the Brusselator's limit cycle and "Turing bifurcation". A closing programme derives irreversibility from a non-unitary transformation of the Liouville dynamics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md)); worth reading as Prigogine's own short statement of the dissipative-structure programme, and as the place where its scope limits are stated in his words. A dissipative structure is a state beyond an instability of the "thermodynamic branch", "a giant fluctuation stabilized by exchanges of energy with the outside world". The minimum-entropy-production theorem is valid only in the "strictly" linear regime with constant phenomenological coefficients. Far from equilibrium the only general criterion offered is a sufficient one for stability (non-negative excess entropy production). Its §§6–7 programme of a non-unitary "entropy operator" is a sketch whose demonstrated link to macroscopic thermodynamics is, by its own account, "at least in the linear region". |
| [LIT-517](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-517.md) | Nonequilibrium Equality for Free Energy Differences | Jarzynski (1997), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevLett.78.2690. For a classical system that starts in canonical equilibrium and is switched from Hamiltonian H_0 to H_1 at any finite rate, the average of e^{−βW} over repetitions equals e^{−βΔF} (Eq. 2), whatever the path and the switching time. The proof is exact for an isolated system and for Nosé–Hoover thermostats, and needs weak coupling for a physical reservoir. Thermodynamic integration and the Zwanzig perturbation formula are its slow and fast limits, and ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF follows by Jensen. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-417](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-417.md)); worth reading as the four-page origin of the nonequilibrium work relation ⟨e^{−βW}⟩ = e^{−βΔF}: an equality, independent of path and switching rate, that turns irreversible work measurements into an equilibrium free-energy difference and gives ⟨W⟩ ≥ ΔF as a corollary by Jensen. Read it knowing two things. The physical-reservoir proof rests on weak coupling (Eq. 9 → 10), which the author states; and its usefulness is limited by the author's own estimate to work fluctuations of order k_BT, so nanoscale systems or simulations. |
| [LIT-518](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-518.md) | Statistical Physics of Adaptation | Perunov, Marsland & England (2014; Phys. Rev. X 2016), arXiv:1412.1875. Starting from a fluctuation relation between coarse-grained macrostates, the paper writes the log-odds of two outcomes of a driven system as an internal-entropy term, a reversal-probability term and Ψ − Φ, the mean heat minus a fluctuation correction (Eq. 8). Holding the first two fixed, the more likely outcome is the one whose formation absorbed and dissipated work from the drive more reliably. It calls such outcomes "adapted" and argues the tendency needs no self-replication. Two single-particle hopping models illustrate the dissipation and fluctuation terms (Eqs. 10–13); the many-body case is a plausibility argument. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-416](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-416.md)), from arXiv v1, the only arXiv version; the published Physical Review X text was not reached. Worth reading as the origin of "dissipative adaptation": the claim that driven matter tends towards states whose formation absorbed and dissipated work reliably, with no replication needed. Read it as a heuristic argument with two toy models, not a theorem. Its exact content is a rearranged macrostate fluctuation relation; the step to "adaptation" holds two terms fixed that it does not show can be held fixed in a many-body system, and the simulation it reports was not shown. It deliberately erases the line between living and non-living organization. |
| [LIT-519](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-519.md) | Nonequilibrium thermodynamics and maximum entropy production in the Earth system | Kleidon (2009), DOI-10.1007/s00114-009-0509-x. A review of MEP in the Earth system. MEP is the proposed principle that a system with enough degrees of freedom adopts the steady state of maximum entropy production. It selects among steady states, where Prigogine's principle only describes relaxation toward one. Box models show the flux–force trade-off that gives an MEP state. The review estimates the Earth's entropy budget, which is dominated by absorption of sunlight. It surveys MEP fits for atmosphere, ocean, mantle, hydrology and biota, and proposes that life drives the planet toward MEP, a thermodynamic reading of Gaia. The author grants that MEP is not established. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-423](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-423.md)); worth reading as the clearest statement of the maximum-entropy-production (MEP) programme in Earth-system science by its main advocate: what MEP claims, how it differs from Prigogine's minimum principle (minimum entropy production describes relaxation toward a steady state; MEP selects among possible steady states), an order-of-magnitude entropy budget of the Earth, a survey of climate, ocean, mantle and biotic MEP applications, and the extension to life and Gaia. Read it as advocacy that is candid about its footing: the author calls MEP "proposed" and says "no one would argue that MEP is well established". Chosen over the Kleidon–Lorenz 2005 book, which has no lawful open text. |
| [LIT-520](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-520.md) v2 | Maximum entropy production principle in physics, chemistry and biology | Martyushev & Seleznev (2006), DOI-10.1016/j.physrep.2005.12.001. A 45-page Physics Reports review of the maximum entropy production principle (MEPP) across physics, chemistry and biology. Kleidon (2009) cites it as the review of MEP's physical foundation. Semantic Scholar's machine-generated summary says it analyses the principle's thermodynamic and statistical basis, including its relation to the second law and to Prigogine's principle. Unread: no text or abstract reached. | Unavailable — seeded 2026-10-02 from Crossref metadata and citing works, not read: no lawful full text or publisher abstract could be reached (Physics Reports, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy, and the abstract is elided by the publisher). Filed because it is the main survey of the maximum-entropy-production principle and of its relation to Prigogine's minimum principle; it stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-521](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-521.md) | Information theory explanation of the fluctuation theorem, maximum entropy production and self-organized criticality in non-equilibrium stationary states | Dewar (2003), DOI-10.1088/0305-4470/36/3/303. It applies Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference to the microscopic paths of an open system in a stationary state. Under fixed initial densities and boundary fluxes plus local conservation, the path distribution is p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ), with A_Γ carrying τσ_Γ/2k_B (Eq. 14). A fluctuation theorem and ⟨σ⟩ ≥ 0 follow (Eqs. 18–21). Then, in a mean-field approximation and assuming the number of paths increases with irreversible action, maximizing path entropy over the remaining multipliers is maximizing mean entropy production (MaxEP, Eq. 24). A Landau–Ginzburg argument claims self-organized criticality as slow driving goes to zero. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-426](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-426.md)); worth reading as the founding attempt to derive the maximum-entropy-production principle (MaxEP) from Jaynes's maximum-entropy inference over microscopic paths, and as the source most later MEP work, Kleidon's included, cites for MEP's theoretical foundation. Read it as a programme, not a proof. The path distribution p_Γ ∝ exp(A_Γ) and its fluctuation theorem follow from the stated constraints. The MaxEP step needs a mean-field approximation and an assumption that the number of paths grows with their irreversible action, which is stated, not argued. The self-organized-criticality corollary is a mean-field artefact by Grinstein and Linsker's analysis ([LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md)), which this reading confirms. |
| [LIT-522](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-522.md) | Entropy production fluctuation theorem and the nonequilibrium work relation for free energy differences | Crooks (1999), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevE.60.2721. For finite classical systems with stochastic, Markovian, microscopically reversible dynamics, the entropy production ω of a forward process and of its time reverse satisfy P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω} for any finite time, provided ω is odd under reversal. That holds for processes that start and end in equilibrium, where ω = β(W − ΔF), and for time-symmetric nonequilibrium steady states. The Jarzynski equality follows in one line, and for long times the theorem gives a heat fluctuation theorem and a Gaussian with variance twice the mean. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-413](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-413.md)); worth reading as the short paper that turned the entropy-production fluctuation theorem into a finite-time, trajectory-level statement for stochastic, microscopically reversible dynamics, P_F(+ω)/P_R(−ω) = e^{ω}, and derived the Jarzynski equality from it in a line. It also defines the trajectory entropy production ω = ln ρ(x_{−τ}) − ln ρ(x_{+τ}) − βQ that the record's stochastic-thermodynamics papers inherit. Read it knowing that its conditions are stated exactly (finite classical system, constant-intensive-parameter baths, Markovian microscopically reversible dynamics, ω odd under time reversal), and that the steady-state version is formally exact but, by the author's own account, of little practical use. |
| [LIT-523](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-523.md) | Stochastic thermodynamics, fluctuation theorems and molecular machines | Seifert (2012), DOI-10.1088/0034-4885/75/12/126001. A 105-page review of stochastic thermodynamics. Work, heat and a stochastic system entropy s = −ln p(x(τ),τ) are defined along single trajectories of Markovian systems coupled to baths, and every known integral, detailed and Crooks fluctuation theorem is derived from one master theorem by choosing a conjugate dynamics. Further results: dissipation bounds forward–reverse distinguishability (⟨w⟩ − ΔF ≥ D[p‖p_eq]), Sagawa–Ueda feedback relations, a NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem in terms of entropy production, and a cycle-based theory of efficiency at maximum power for molecular machines. | Active — read 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-420](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-420.md); §§5, 8.3–8.4, 9.2 and 11 skimmed); worth reading as the systematic reference for stochastic thermodynamics as of 2012: first law, heat and stochastic entropy along single trajectories of Markovian systems coupled to baths, every known fluctuation theorem derived from one master theorem with a conjugate dynamics, dissipation as distinguishability of forward and reverse paths, Sagawa–Ueda feedback, the NESS fluctuation–dissipation theorem and efficiency of molecular machines. It is the framework in which the record's thermodynamics-of-prediction and thermodynamics-of-learning results ([LIT-327](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-327.md), [LIT-308](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-308.md)) are stated. Read it as a review: the derivations are its own and concise, the case studies are reported. |
| [LIT-524](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-524.md) v2 | Self-Organization in Nonequilibrium Systems: From Dissipative Structures to Order through Fluctuations | Nicolis & Prigogine (1977), Wiley-Interscience. The Brussels school's monograph on self-organization far from equilibrium, from the thermodynamics and bifurcation theory of dissipative structures to their stochastic theory ("order through fluctuations"). The Nobel lecture cites its ch. VII for the Brusselator and the book for its catalogue of chemical and biological examples. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scan is a lending-only copy, HathiTrust is search-only, and no publisher description or table of contents was found), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the Brussels school's book-length treatment of dissipative structures and "order through fluctuations", and the source the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)) gives for the Brusselator; what it contains beyond that is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-525](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-525.md) | Comments on a derivation and application of the ‘maximum entropy production’ principle | Grinstein & Linsker (2007), DOI-10.1088/1751-8113/40/31/N01. A Comment with two points. (1) Dewar's 2005 derivation of MaxEP needs a quadratic approximation to p(f) near f = F to hold for all f. With the fluctuation theorem, that forces A(F) to be constant, i.e. linear constitutive relations. So the "orthogonality condition" behind both maximum and minimum entropy production fails far from equilibrium, as an exact spin-chain model shows. (2) Dewar's 2003 SOC result is an artefact. Keeping the quartic term gives a finite flux variance at F_ext = 0. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-422](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-422.md)); worth reading as the short, exact critique of Dewar's information-theoretic derivation of maximum entropy production. It shows that the 2005 derivation's key step holds only where the constitutive relations are linear, so MaxEP far from equilibrium is not established by it, and that the 2003 claim that MaxEP yields self-organized criticality is an artefact of a mean-field expansion. Read from the authors' submitted manuscript (Zenodo); the version of record was not seen. Its first point is checked here only on its own worked example, since Dewar 2005 itself could not be read. |
| [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) | Life as we know it | Friston (2013), J. R. Soc. Interface 10(86):20130475. Any ergodic random dynamical system whose states split into internal, sensory, active and external sets with a Markov blanket has internal and active states whose flow can be written as a gradient descent on a variational free energy of the blanket and internal states (Lemma 2.1, Eqs. 2.5–2.8). They therefore "appear" to do Bayesian inference about external states and to bound their own entropy. A simulated "primordial soup" of 128 coupled Lorenz subsystems forms a blanket-enclosed cluster whose internal states predict external motion (5 of 82 above a time-reversed null) and which disperses when blanket or internal states are lesioned. The paper says a candle flame cannot have a Markov blanket, and concedes that the universe holds countless blankets, conjecturing that minimum-entropy blankets mark life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-421](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-421.md)), from the published text (the author's posted PDF of the journal version and the PMC full text). Worth reading as the founding statement of the Markov-blanket formulation of the free energy principle applied to life, and as the one text in the record that names a candle flame and says it is not lifelike. Read it as a redescription, not a derivation: its "heuristic proof" shows that the flow of an ergodic system with a Markov blanket can be written as a gradient flow on a variational free energy, by choosing the variational density to equal the posterior. The free energy is variational, not thermodynamic; no heat or entropy production is computed. The simulation is one run, analysed with a blanket chosen by spectral clustering. |
| [LIT-527](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-527.md) | Pattern formation outside of equilibrium | Cross & Hohenberg (1993), DOI-10.1103/RevModPhys.65.851. A 262-page review classifying non-equilibrium patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state: type I_s (finite wave-number, stationary: convection rolls, Turing patterns), III_o (uniform oscillation: the stirred BZ reaction) and I_o (travelling waves). Near threshold, universal amplitude equations describe them, and phase equations describe them further above it. It finds no general variational principle for non-equilibrium steady states, only perturbative ones near threshold. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-418](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-418.md)), about 30 of 262 pages read closely; worth reading as the physicists' standard account of pattern formation away from equilibrium, and as the sober counterweight to the dissipative-structure programme. It treats Rayleigh–Bénard convection, Turing patterns and the BZ reaction in one framework, classifying patterns by the linear instability of a uniform state and describing them near onset by universal amplitude equations. Its conclusion finds "no evidence for the existence of any global minimization principles controlling the structure, except as a perturbative statement near threshold", and quotes Glansdorff and Prigogine conceding as much. |
| [LIT-528](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-528.md) | Energy flow and the organization of life | Morowitz & Smith (2006 working paper; Complexity 2007). Life may be forced into existence by abiotic free-energy sources, as lightning and hurricanes are channels that relieve electric and thermal potentials. Core anabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle and the cascade built on it, is read as a relaxation channel for geochemical redox and phosphate energy. Jaynes-style entropy maximization with current-dependent entropies (not entropy-production principles) is offered as the framework, and the emergence of life as a "collapse", a phase transition of a metastable abiotic earth. Selection on metabolism comes before replication. No quantitative model is given; the authors say the claim is undemonstrated. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-425](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-425.md)), from the Santa Fe Institute working paper (2006-08-029, dated 7 August 2006), not the Complexity version of record. Filed in place of Morowitz's 1968 book Energy Flow in Biology, which could not be read: every Internet Archive scan of it is lending-only. Worth reading as a short statement of the "life was inevitable" view by Morowitz and Smith: core metabolism, the reductive citric-acid cycle, is a channel geochemistry was forced to open to relieve free-energy stresses, as lightning relieves a charge separation. It is an essay. It says itself that the claim "has not been quantitatively demonstrated", and its evidence is the structure of core metabolism read in that light. It puts life on a continuum with lightning and hurricanes and draws no principled line. |
| [LIT-530](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-530.md) v2 | What Is Life? The Physical Aspect of the Living Cell | Schrödinger (1944), Cambridge University Press. Lectures given at Trinity College Dublin in February 1943, published as a short book for the lay reader. It asks how events inside a living organism can be accounted for by physics and chemistry. It treats the gene as an "aperiodic crystal" carrying a code-script, defended through the Delbrück model, and in chapter 6 says an organism keeps its order by drawing "order from order" and by feeding on negative entropy from its surroundings. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and contents; the text itself was not reached. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Cambridge Core contents and chapter excerpts, and library catalogue records, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The book is in copyright with Cambridge University Press. Every Internet Archive scan of a Cambridge or Macmillan printing is lending-only, and the freely downloadable PDFs that turn up (course sites, personal uploads, Internet Archive "opensource" uploads) are unauthorized copies of the Canto edition, so I did not open them. Chapter 6, the negative-entropy chapter, is unread beyond the publisher's one-paragraph excerpt. |
| [LIT-531](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-531.md) | Belousov-Zhabotinsky reaction | Zhabotinsky (2007), Scholarpedia 2(9):1435. BZ reactions are metal-ion-catalysed oxidations of organic reductants by bromate in acid. The core loop is autocatalytic oxidation of the catalyst via HBrO₂, switched off by bromide, which the oxidized catalyst regenerates from bromomalonic acid. Closed, stirred, it can run "up to several thousand" cycles; only in a continuous-flow reactor do oscillations continue indefinitely, and there bursting and chaos appear. Unstirred thin layers support target and spiral waves (Zaikin & Zhabotinsky 1970). The Oregonator is qualitatively right and quantitatively not. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-414](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-414.md)); worth reading as the short, authoritative account of the Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction by the chemist who named half of it: discovery, the core mechanism (autocatalytic HBrO₂ inhibited by Br⁻), the Oregonator and its known defects, closed versus open-reactor dynamics, and target and spiral waves. Chosen over Zaikin & Zhabotinsky (1970) because it is openly readable and covers the 1970 waves paper; it is a short encyclopedia review with no new results. |
| [LIT-532](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-532.md) v2 | Inadequacy of entropy and entropy derivatives in characterizing the steady state | Landauer (1975), DOI-10.1103/PhysRevA.12.636. Per its abstract: in a bistable system the kinetics of transitions between the two locally stable states can be changed without changing the behaviour near either state, so no quantity that characterises only the vicinity of the states can determine which is more probable. Separately, even a monostable linear circuit's steady state need not be one of minimum entropy production. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Unavailable — seeded 2026-10-02 from its abstract and Crossref metadata, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (Physical Review A, closed; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex list no open copy). Filed because it is the classic objection to entropy-based characterisations of nonequilibrium steady states, Prigogine's minimum principle among them; it stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-533](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-533.md) | Life as a manifestation of the second law of thermodynamics | Schneider & Kay (1994), Math. Comput. Modelling 19(6–8):25–48. A "restated second law": systems moved from equilibrium "utilize all avenues available to counter the applied gradients". Bénard convection and a vortex draining a bottle are read as structures that destroy gradients faster. Life is "another means of dissipating the solar induced gradient" (living systems as "sophisticated mini-tornados, with a memory"), and ecosystems develop to degrade more incoming exergy. A stressed marsh shows smaller flows and fewer cycles; airborne thermal scans show mature forests cooler (degrading 90% of net solar radiation against a quarry's 62%). The second law is "necessary but not sufficient" for life. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-415](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-415.md)), from the authors' own formatted text (copyright line "James J. Kay and Eric Schneider, 1992"), not the journal's typeset version. Worth reading as the canonical statement of the "gradient-dissipation" view of life: living systems and ecosystems are dissipative structures that develop so as to degrade the solar gradient more completely, and the second law is "a necessary but not sufficient cause for life". Read the thermodynamics as a programme, not a derivation. The "restated second law" is offered as a corollary of Kestin's stability result but not derived from it. The ecological evidence is one stressed-versus-control marsh pair and a few thermal-scanner and satellite comparisons, all correlational. It draws no line between living and non-living dissipative structures beyond "memory" (DNA). |
| [LIT-534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-534.md) v2 | Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature | Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Bantam; based on their La nouvelle alliance. A book for general readers that sets the science of complexity and irreversibility against classical dynamics. By its contents: the rise and limits of Newtonian science and its philosophical reception (Diderot, Kant, Hegel, Bergson, Whitehead); thermodynamics from Carnot to Boltzmann's order principle; linear and far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics, bifurcations and order through fluctuations; and the rediscovery of time in physics. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and a partial contents note; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the Bantam and Flamingo printings are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the popular and philosophical statement of the programme whose technical core is the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)); what it argues, beyond its contents, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-535](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-535.md) | The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis | Turing (1952), DOI-10.1098/rstb.1952.0012. Chemicals ("morphogens") that react and diffuse through tissue can turn a stable homogeneous state unstable, with random disturbances setting which pattern grows. On a ring of cells the linearized onset takes six forms. The most important is stationary waves of finite "chemical wave-length", which (9.4a, b) allow for two morphogens only if they diffuse at different rates. A 20-cell example computed on the Manchester computer gives a three-lobed pattern. Hydra tentacles, whorled leaves, dappling and gastrulation are suggested applications, not tested ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-427](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-427.md)); worth reading as the founding paper of reaction–diffusion pattern formation and the origin of what the Brussels school later called the "Turing bifurcation". A homogeneous, stable steady state of reacting and diffusing chemicals can be destabilized by diffusion itself and settle into a stationary pattern with an intrinsic "chemical wave-length". The analysis is linear and near onset by design, every biological application is offered as suggestion, and the paper says outright that its patterns are "dynamic equilibria" fed by "a continual supply of free energy", which places them among dissipative structures before the term existed. |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) v4 | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Only the Introduction is read ([NOTE-1437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1437.md)): there the authors make closure of constraints the core of biological organisation, say it differs fundamentally from the self-organisation of dissipative structures, and announce that it grounds teleology, normativity and function; the chapters that argue this are unread. | Unfetched — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list. The book is not open access at Springer. Its only free copy, the authors' HAL deposit (hal-01151449, hal.science/hal-01151449/document, CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015), is not the whole book, as this note earlier said: it holds the front matter (Hooker's Foreword and the contents), the Introduction (pp. xix–xxxiv), the references and the index, and no chapter. The Introduction was read in full on 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1437](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1437.md), Skimmed, because only the Introduction was read). II), the second-order excess entropy δ²S as a Lyapounov function near equilibrium (ch. V), and the excess-entropy-production criterion far from equilibrium, including convection (ch. VII). Three conditions are jointly necessary and sufficient for minimal agency: the system defines its own individuality, it is the active source of modulations of its coupling with the environment (interactional asymmetry), and it regulates that coupling by norms it generates (normativity). Generatively, an agent is an open autonomous system (a precarious network of mutually enabling processes) that adaptively modulates its coupling so as to maintain some of its constituent processes. Minimal life satisfies this; life is sufficient for agency but not necessary. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-458](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-458.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the standard organizational definition of minimal agency, and as the clearest statement that an agent is not the same thing as an individual. Individuality is one of three conditions, with interactional asymmetry and normativity; it is a precondition for the other two and is not sufficient for agency. The generative definition: an agent is an autonomous organization that adaptively regulates its coupling with its environment and contributes to sustaining itself as a consequence. The paper rejects statistical and energetic measures of asymmetry as sufficient, and says systems optimising an externally fixed function should not be treated as models of agency. |
| [LIT-570](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-570.md) | An Organizational Account of Biological Functions | Mossio, Saborido & Moreno (2009), BJPS 60(4):813–841. A trait has a function iff it contributes to the maintenance of a self-maintaining organization, is produced and maintained under that organization's constraints, and the organization is differentiated. Worth reading as the organizational account of function and as the place where the organizational school says plainly that a candle flame has closure. Functions are contributions to a differentiated self-maintaining organization by traits that organization produces and maintains. Closure alone grounds teleology and norms but is shared by flames, Bénard cells and hurricanes; organizational differentiation is what functions need. Reproduction is admitted to be a problem and left to a sketch. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md) v3 | A theoretical model of phase transitions in human hand movements | Haken, Kelso & Bunz (1985), Biological Cybernetics 51(5):347–356. Models the involuntary switch from anti-phase to in-phase finger or hand movement as movement frequency rises: relative phase φ is the order parameter, φ̇ = −∂V/∂φ with V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ, both patterns are stable while \|b\| > \|a\|/4 and only in-phase below it, and hysteresis follows. The φ equation is derived from two self-sustained oscillators whose coupling must be nonlinear, with amplitude falling as frequency rises acting as the control. A theory paper: its data are Kelso's earlier experiments, summarized. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1424.md)) in full, from the publisher's scan posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/1985_Haken_Kelso_Bunz_Biol_Cyb.pdf); worth reading as the paper that states the HKB model: relative phase as order parameter, the potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ with anti-phase lost when b/a falls below 1/4, and its derivation from two nonlinearly coupled limit-cycle oscillators. Read it knowing that it is a theory paper with one numerical simulation and no new data: the switch and the hysteresis it models are summarized from Kelso's earlier experiments, and critical fluctuations and critical slowing are named as future work, not reported. |

HKB models bimanual coordination by the relative phase φ, with dφ/dt = −a sin φ − 2b sin 2φ and potential V = −a cos φ − b cos 2φ: both in-phase and anti-phase are stable for b/a > 1/4, and anti-phase loses stability below it, as observed when movement frequency rises. The same dynamics is reported within a body, between people and with machines, and in brain activity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-467](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-467.md)), from the free-to-read publisher PDF. Filed in place of Kelso's book Dynamic Patterns ([LIT-578](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-578.md)) and as the read account of the paywalled Haken–Kelso–Bunz paper ([LIT-588](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-588.md)), both Deferred. Worth reading as Kelso's own short statement of coordination dynamics: the HKB order-parameter equation for relative phase, its stochastic and symmetry-breaking extensions, metastability as relative coordination, the generalized HKB–Kuramoto model, and the claim that one coordination dynamics holds within and between people. It is a retrospective by an author of the model, not a review, and it says so. |

Unread: registered from the abstract and the reference list. | Unavailable — registered 2026-10-03 from the abstract, keywords and reference list, not read. The article is closed access at Elsevier. Consciousness occurs when mind contents are spontaneously identified as belonging to their organism, and a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings (hunger, pain, well-being, plain feelings of existence) supplies that identification and "lends" consciousness to exteroceptive images. Feelings are hybrid: interoceptive pathways are unmyelinated, partly non-synaptic and unprotected by a blood–brain barrier, so the body and its neural map interact directly. Posterior brainstem lesions abolish consciousness where large cortical ones may not; consciousness needs "a partnership of nervous systems with the bodies they serve". | Active — skimmed 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-507](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-507.md)): every section was covered, but through a fetch tool that returned section-by-section accounts with short quotes, not a verbatim copy, so the quotes are unchecked; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Damasios' claim that consciousness is the spontaneous identification of mind contents as one's own, supplied by a continuous flow of homeostatic feelings, which are hybrid: in interoception the map and the body it maps interact and "commingle". It is a five-page Essay with no data. Its evidence is clinical and cited (brainstem coma versus cortical lesions, general anaesthesia), and its mechanism is the cellular contrast in Table 1: unmyelinated, non-synaptic, barrier-free interoceptive pathways. |

Modelling tryptophan 1La transition dipoles in tubulin architectures with a radiative non-Hermitian Hamiltonian in the single-excitation limit, the authors predict strongly superradiant states (up to about 4000 times the single-tryptophan rate in a centriole, about 7000 extrapolated for large axon-like bundles) and a thermal quantum yield that rises with network size and survives static disorder of room-temperature size. A coral is a consortium: the animal plus the Symbiodiniaceae, bacteria, archaea, fungi and viruses in its body, mucus and skeleton, and neighbours are excluded by definition. Traits such as thermal tolerance belong to the host–symbiont combination: not every Durusdinium is heat tolerant, and a novel anemone–alga pairing gave higher oxygen flux under heat than both natural ones. Measuring both partners shows different routes to the same bleaching outcome. The physiological evidence it cites is thin and partly not from corals: its one demonstration that a combination is "not necessarily the sum of its parts" is an oxygen-flux experiment in the sea anemone Exaiptasia. A second experiment found that blue, green and white nocturnal light delayed spawning by 6–8 h or 2 nights and red light did not. Worth reading as the controlled experiment behind the claim that reef recovery after bleaching depends on an ecological interaction, not only on surviving corals. On an inshore Great Barrier Reef crest after the 1998 bleaching, roofless cages kept large and medium fishes out of four 25 m² plots for 30 months. Macroalgae rose to a mean of 56% cover in the cages against 4.1% and 1.7% in partial cages and open plots. In Poisson algebras, complex *-algebras and Banach–Lie algebras, "a generates symmetries of b iff b generates symmetries of a" follows from the antisymmetry of the bracket and uniqueness of solutions; for a bilinear bracket, antisymmetry is the self-conservation principle {a, a} = 0. The content lies in identifying observables with generators; in quantum theory that identification is multiplication by i, and Alfsen and Shultz's dynamical correspondence recovers it from a JB-algebra under the self-conservation principle and a second condition that Baez reads as "inverse temperature is imaginary time". The paper proves nothing new, by its own statement. |

In single-cell swarm assays (over 10,000 plates), an E. coli cell's swarming potential is shared by its fourth-generation descendants and lost by the seventh; it tracks the cell's iron status (low iron, better swarmer), iron starvation or forced uptake lengthens it, and a three-state switching model fits the lineages only with a fixed holding delay before switching. In Boolean models of the E. coli transcriptional regulatory network, a transient single-gene knockout or overexpression often moves the network to a different attractor, so one genotype can hold several heritable expression states without epigenetic marks. Model only: the paper runs no transient-perturbation experiment. Its one comparison with data, against strains evolved after a permanent crp knockout, mostly tests the sign structure of the network, and its link to irreversibility is weak (P = 0.03 on small counts). |
| [LIT-872](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-872.md) | Hyperbolic geometry of the olfactory space | Zhou, Smith & Sharpee (2018), Science Advances 4(8):eaaq1458. In four natural odour sources the rank order of correlations between compound concentrations has the clique-topology signature of points near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball and not of a uniform Euclidean cube, and human perceptual descriptions of 127 odorants have that of a full 3D hyperbolic ball. Pleasantness, boiling point and acidity read out as linear axes of the fitted fruit-odour space. The hierarchy that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued from biochemistry, not recovered from the data. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-672](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-672.md)); worth reading as the first application of clique topology to stimulus statistics rather than neural data, and as the Sharpee lab's first claim of a hyperbolic geometry in biology. For four natural odour sources (strawberry, tomato, blueberry, mouse urine; 45–78 compounds over 50–101 samples), the rank order of absolute concentration correlations gives Betti curves that match points sampled near the surface of a 3D hyperbolic ball (R_max = 7, R_min = 0.9 R_max, the same for all four) and reject uniform Euclidean cubes of any dimension tried. Human descriptor profiles for 127 odorants (Dravnieks) match a full 3D hyperbolic ball and no Euclidean cube. Linear axes for pleasantness, boiling point and acidity are found in the fitted fruit-odour space. The tree that motivates the hyperbolic model is argued, not recovered: compounds do not cluster by chemical class, and the only null geometry is a uniform Euclidean cube. |
| [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) v2 | Mutual information, neural networks and the renormalization group | Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2017; Nature Physics 14, 578–582, 2018). Defines the relevant degrees of freedom of a spatial block as the coarse variable that maximizes mutual information with the environment beyond a buffer, and learns it with restricted Boltzmann machines from Monte Carlo samples (the RSMI algorithm). It recovers Kadanoff block spins in the 2D Ising model and the electric-field variables of the dimer model, ignores decoupled noise, and, iterated, gives the Ising flow and ν ≈ 1.0 ± 0.15; a distribution-fitting RBM does none of this. The link to a short-ranged effective Hamiltonian is proved only in 1D. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-674](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-674.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns "the relevant degrees of freedom" of real-space renormalization into an objective that can be optimized: a block's coarse variable is chosen to maximize its mutual information with the system beyond a buffer around the block. Trained on Monte Carlo samples alone, the network rediscovers Kadanoff's block spin for the 2D Ising model, finds the low-momentum electric fields of the 2D dimer model while ignoring a strongly patterned but decoupled noise, and, iterated, reproduces the Ising flow away from T_c (located to about 1%) with ν ≈ 1.0 ± 0.15. An RBM trained instead to fit the data distribution latches on to the noise. The equivalence of the objective with a short-ranged effective Hamiltonian is argued, and shown only for 1D and quasi-1D chains; in 2D the evidence is the two models, whose answers were known beforehand. |
| [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md) v2 | Statistical Physics through the Lens of Real-Space Mutual Information | Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2021; Phys. Rev. Lett. 127, 240603). Replaces the RBM estimator of [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) with a neural InfoNCE lower bound co-trained with a convolutional coarse-graining filter (RSMI-NE), and uses the optimal filters at a single buffer size, not an iterated flow, as lattice forms of the most relevant operators. On the interacting dimer model they are the columnar and plaquette order parameters below T_BKT and the electric fields at high T; the maximal information marks the phases; one fitted scaling dimension (1.00037 against 1) is given. The optimality theorem is cited, not proved here. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-681](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-681.md)); worth reading as the paper that turns the real-space mutual-information principle of [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) from an iterated coarse-graining into a single-shot extraction of operators: with the mutual information estimated by a neural InfoNCE bound and the coarse-graining a convolutional filter trained against it, the filters that best compress what a block shares with its distant environment are, across the whole phase diagram of the interacting dimer model, the columnar and plaquette order parameters below the BKT transition and the electric fields at high temperature, and the plaquette filter's correlator gives a scaling dimension of 1.00037 against the predicted 1. The maximal information itself, log 4 in the ordered phase and decaying algebraically with the buffer in the critical one, traces the phase diagram. The theorem that the optimal filters are the most relevant operators is cited to another paper, and the model's operators were known beforehand. |
| [LIT-881](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-881.md) v2 | Optimal Renormalization Group Transformation from Information Theory | Lenggenhager, Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2018; Phys. Rev. X 10, 011037, 2020). Proves that a block coarse-graining keeping all the mutual information the block shares with the system beyond a buffer makes the coarse measure factorize across the block, so a finite-range Hamiltonian gains no range (1D; D dimensions under an extra assumption) and 1D disorder gains no correlations across it. For blocks of two spins of the 1D clean and dilute random Ising chain, where that condition is not met, couplings beyond nearest neighbour and disorder correlations shrink as more information is kept, vanishing at decimation. Encoding into a single binary spin explains why decimation wins in 1D and majority rule in a 2D toy model. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-682](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-682.md)); worth reading as the theory written for the RSMI algorithm of LIT-873: it proves that a coarse-graining which keeps all the information a block shares with the system beyond a buffer factorizes the coarse measure across that block, so a finite-range Hamiltonian does not gain range (in 1D; in D dimensions under an extra per-block assumption) and, for 1D disorder, no correlations are generated across the block. The full-capture condition is not met by the coarse-grainings it then studies: in its own 1D Ising example decimation keeps about half of the block's information, and the decay of next-nearest-neighbour and four-spin couplings, and of disorder correlations, as information grows is shown numerically for blocks of two spins. Its other result is information-theoretic: a single binary block spin loses information by encoding, which is why decimation beats majority rule in 1D and majority rule wins in a 2D toy model. |
| [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) | An exact mapping between the Variational Renormalization Group and Deep Learning | Mehta and Schwab (2014), arXiv preprint, never published in a journal. Identifies Kadanoff's variational RG kernel with an RBM's energy by T = −E + H, under which the coarse-grained Hamiltonian is the RBM's hidden-marginal Hamiltonian for any parameters and an exact RG step is a perfect fit of the data. Illustrates it with a hand-built decimation network for the 1D Ising chain and a four-layer stacked RBM trained on 2D Ising samples near T_c, whose receptive fields are local and grow with depth. It concedes that, short of exactness, RG and RBM training use different variational schemes; [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) shows the difference matters. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-683](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-683.md)); worth reading as the paper that first put deep restricted Boltzmann machines and Kadanoff's variational renormalization group side by side, and as the position Koch-Janusz and Ringel ([LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md)) argue against. Its "exact mapping" is an identification: setting the RG kernel T = −E + H makes the coarse-grained Hamiltonian equal the RBM's hidden-marginal Hamiltonian for every parameter value, and makes an exact RG step the same thing as a perfect fit of the data distribution. Away from that point the paper itself says the two procedures use different variational approximations, so the mapping does not show that training an RBM performs RG. The evidence that it does is a hand-built 1D decimation network and qualitative receptive fields of a stacked RBM on 2D Ising samples; no flow, fixed point or exponent is computed. |
| [LIT-885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-885.md) | Relevance in the Renormalization Group and in Information Theory | Gordon, Banerjee, Koch-Janusz and Ringel (2020; Phys. Rev. Lett. 126, 240601, 2021). On a cylinder, with block and environment as slabs separated by a buffer of length L_B, the information-bottleneck encoder just past its first transition depends on the block only through the boundary weak value of the leading transfer-matrix eigenvector, the lowest-dimension primary at large circumference, and the transition is at β_c = (λ0/λ1)^(2L_B). Checked on a three-site critical Ising cylinder. With a large enough alphabet the encoder respects the data's symmetry near that transition; a small one can break it. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-690](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-690.md)); worth reading as the theorem the real-space mutual-information programme ([LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md), [LIT-881](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-881.md), [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md)) cites for its claim that the optimal coarse-graining picks out the most relevant operators. What it proves is narrower than that claim: for a short-range lattice model on a cylinder, with the block and the environment taken as whole slabs of the cylinder separated by a buffer, the information-bottleneck encoder just past its first transition depends on the block only through the boundary weak value of the leading transfer-matrix eigenvector, and the transition sits at β_c = (λ0/λ1)^(2L_B); for large circumference that eigenvector is the lowest-dimension primary. The planar block-in-a-shell geometry the algorithms use, the fixed-alphabet β → ∞ limit that is RSMI, and the regime beyond the first transition are not covered. A second result: past the first transition, with a large enough alphabet and no fine-tuning, the optimal encoder carries a representation of the data's symmetry, and a two-symbol example with Z4 symmetry breaks it. |
| [LIT-887](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-887.md) v2 | Why does deep and cheap learning work so well? | Lin, Tegmark and Rolnick (2016; Journal of Statistical Physics 168, 1223–1247, 2017). Argues that networks are cheap because physical data have low-order, local, symmetric Hamiltonians, and deep because data come from Markov generative hierarchies whose minimal sufficient statistics compose. Proves that a single hidden layer needs exactly 2^n neurons to multiply n inputs, against about 4n in a deep tree, and gives linear no-flattening examples. Holds that RG is supervised feature extraction, not unsupervised learning; arXiv v1–v2 carried a counterexample against [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) that hit a typo in its Eq. 8, and was dropped later. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-688](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-688.md)); worth reading as the third position in the dispute over whether deep learning performs renormalization, and for two results that stand on their own. On the dispute it holds that RG is "essentially a feature extractor for supervised learning": a coarse-graining is a renormalization only once the variables to keep are specified, and fitting the data distribution does not specify them. That holds, and it agrees with what [LIT-882](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-882.md) concedes and [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) shows; its sharper form was in an appendix of arXiv v1 and v2 only, dropped from v3 on and from the journal text, showing that a matched partition function does not give a matched distribution and (v2) that the exact trace condition is met by hidden variables that do not interact with the system at all. Its conclusion that RG has "little to do" with unsupervised learning is too strong: [LIT-873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-873.md) gets the relevant variables without labels, from the far environment. On its own merits: a two-variable product needs four neurons and an n-variable product needs exactly 2^n in one hidden layer against about 4n in a deep tree (proved, in a Taylor-matching sense, with weights that grow without bound); the minimal sufficient statistics of a Markov generative hierarchy compose level by level (proved, and nearly immediate); that physics favours low-order, local, symmetric Hamiltonians, and that this is why cheap networks work, is argued, not shown. |
| [LIT-889](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-889.md) v2 | Symmetries and phase diagrams with real-space mutual information neural estimation | Gökmen, Ringel, Huber and Koch-Janusz (2021; Phys. Rev. E 104, 064106), the long companion of [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md). Derives the RSMI-NE estimator in full and applies it to the 2D Ising model (1 bit below T_c, exponential decay with the buffer above it, boundary filters at T_c), the interacting dimer model and a 1D non-equilibrium chipping model. Its new object is the ensemble of optimal filters from independent runs: it maps an RSMI-degenerate subspace whose projections show broken and emergent (U(1)) symmetries, and PCA of it recovers the pristine operators. Every model's answer was known beforehand. | Active — read 2026-10-09 ([NOTE-692](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-692.md)); worth reading as the long companion of [LIT-878](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-878.md) and the place where the real-space mutual-information method is shown on more than one model and its outputs are read as an ensemble: the maximal information counts the ordered sectors (exactly 1 bit in the 2D Ising ferromagnet, 2 bits in the columnar dimer phase), decays exponentially with the buffer in the Ising paramagnet and algebraically at criticality, and the optimal Ising filter goes uniform, boundary and random across T_c; 500 independent runs per temperature map an RSMI-degenerate subspace of filters whose projections show the broken C4 and translation symmetries of the dimer model and, at high temperature, its emergent U(1), and PCA of the ensemble recovers the pristine operators from a window where they never appear alone. The number of coarse variables is chosen where the information stops growing. A non-equilibrium chipping model is a one-figure validation, and its formal status is said to be missing. |
| [LIT-891](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-891.md) | Comment on "Why does deep and cheap learning work so well?" | Schwab and Mehta (2016), arXiv comment, never published elsewhere. | [LIT-919](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-919.md) v2 | Nucleation | Vekilov (2010), Cryst. Growth Des. 10, 5007. For lysozyme, nucleation rates are about ten orders of magnitude below the classical prediction, and the paper places the error in the prefactor. The mechanism is inferred from a fitted model for one protein. | Active — read in full 2026-10-11 ([NOTE-708](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-708.md)), from the NIHPA author manuscript at PMC2995260; worth reading as the line's one clear statement, in a single paper, of classical nucleation theory (n* = 64Ω²α³/Δμ³, ΔG* = 32Ω²α³/Δμ²), of where it fails, and of the two things the author puts beside it: a solution–crystal spinodal, past which the nucleus is one molecule and there is no barrier, and the two-step mechanism, in which crystals nucleate inside metastable dense-liquid clusters that form fast, so that ordering inside them is the slow step. For metastable clusters the mechanism is inferred from a fitted kinetic model, not observed, and the claim that substrates act on the prefactor rather than the barrier is argued, not measured. | [LIT-920](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-920.md) v2 | Studien über die Bildung und Umwandlung fester Körper. 1. Abhandlung: Übersättigung und Überkaltung | Ostwald (1897), Z. Phys. Chem. 22, 289. Measures how small a seed can be (about 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹² g) and shows that only the solid itself or a strictly isomorphous solid seeds; separates metastable states (change only on contact with the new phase) from labile ones (spontaneous change); and states the rule later called the rule of stages: on leaving a state spontaneously, the form reached is the nearest in free energy, not the most stable. Offered as a frequent rule, not a law. | Active — read in full 2026-10-11 ([NOTE-709](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-709.md)), in German, from the public-domain scan of the volume at the Internet Archive; worth reading as the primary source of the rule later called the rule of stages, and of the metastable/labile distinction. Read §§26–41 (pp. 301–313): the definitions on p. 302, the rule on pp. 306–307 ("nicht der ... stabilste ..., sondern der nächstliegende"), and the conditional on p. 308 that a metastable intermediate stays until seeded unless it is labile with respect to the next form. Ostwald offers it "not as a law" but as "a frequently applicable rule" (p. 308), from a handful of cases and an analogy with the liquid–vapour isotherm, and absorbs exceptions by assuming unseen intermediates, a move he calls questionable (p. 309). Most of the paper measures seeds: only the solid or a strictly isomorphous solid seeds, down to about 10⁻⁹–10⁻¹² g. For du/dt = Au with A non-normal, the eigenvalues fix only the t → ∞ behaviour. Growth over time t is the top singular value of e^{At}, set at t → 0 by the numerical abscissa, the top eigenvalue of (A + A†)/2. Systems with every mode damped amplify perturbations by large factors before decaying, and their forced and white-noise responses exceed the equivalent normal response. Worked in a 2 × 2 example and damped Eady models. | Active — read 2026-10-14 ([NOTE-831](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-831.md)) in full; worth reading as the compact statement of non-modal stability for a fixed linear operator: growth over a finite time is the top singular value of the propagator, the eigenvalues govern only the long-run limit, and forced and stochastic responses exceed those of the normal system with the same spectrum. | [LIT-932](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-932.md) v2 | Hydrodynamic Stability Without Eigenvalues | Trefethen et al. (1993), Science 261, 578. Plane Couette and Poiseuille flow become turbulent at Reynolds numbers where eigenvalue analysis says they are stable. The proof modifies Isett's: a gluing step whose Reynolds stress stays trace-free, then Mikado-flow perturbations placed in disjoint "squiggling" space-time regions that cover every time, so energy can be pumped in even where the stress vanishes. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1013](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1013.md)) in full, from arXiv:1701.08678v1: worth reading for the admissible half of Onsager's negative direction: for every β < 1/3 and every smooth, strictly positive energy profile e(t) on [0, T] there is a weak solution of the 3D incompressible Euler equations on the periodic box, Hölder-continuous with exponent β in space and time, whose energy ∫\|v\|² equals e(t) at every time; taking e strictly decreasing gives solutions whose kinetic energy strictly decreases, so the energy flux into vanishing scales is one-signed on every time interval ([THEORY-776](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-776.md)); and for a shorter, more self-contained proof of the 1/3 threshold than Isett's ([LIT-1255](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1255.md)), with a trace-free glued stress and perturbations added everywhere in time so as to steer the energy. Read it knowing that "admissible" here means only that the total energy does not increase (the word appears in the title alone), not the local energy inequality, so the transfer is one-way for the whole box and may run backwards in places; that the same theorem gives solutions with increasing energy just as readily, so the direction is chosen by the prescribed profile and is not forced by the equations; that nothing is shown about vanishing-viscosity limits, about uniqueness or non-uniqueness for given initial data, or about the endpoint 1/3; that the h-principle (Theorem 1.3) rests on a result of Daneri and Székelyhidi stated without proof; and that the abstract's "typical" is looser than the weak-* density that Theorem 1.3 proves. |
| [LIT-1304](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1304.md) v2 | Discrete approach to stochastic parametrization and dimension reduction in nonlinear dynamics | Chorin & Lu (PNAS 2015). Proposes model reduction done entirely in discrete time: the resolved variables are advanced by a fixed numerical scheme plus a discrepancy sequence computed exactly from data, and the discrepancy is fitted as a NARMAX time series (autoregression in itself, lags of functions of the resolved variables, moving average in past innovations). Memory is thereby carried by finitely many lags. The connection to Mori–Zwanzig is drawn by analogy, not derived. On two-scale Lorenz 96 with ε = 0.5, a fit with one autoregressive lag, one or two exogenous lags and at most one moving-average term reproduces the statistics of x₁ better than a polynomial-plus-AR(1) closure, and at observation spacing 0.05 extends the lead time at anomaly correlation 0.6 from 2 to 4. | [LIT-1305](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1305.md) v2 | Nonuniqueness and existence of continuous, globally dissipative Euler flows | Isett (2017; Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis 2022). For every α < 1/15 there are weak solutions of the incompressible Euler equations on T³ (and T^d, d ≥ 3) in C^α_{t,x} that satisfy the local energy inequality ∂_t(\|v\|²/2) + ∇·((\|v\|²/2 + p)v) ≤ 0, strictly on an open time interval: the first continuous examples, and a first partial result on the strong Onsager conjecture. From one initial datum there is a Cantor family of them, with no isolated points, positive Hausdorff dimension in C_tL²_x and one common dissipation measure; the same holds for solutions with the local energy equality, and wild data are C⁰ dense. The scheme is a convex integration of "dissipative Euler–Reynolds flows" with one-directional transported plane waves, whose triad interactions cancel the unresolved energy flux current. In the proof the dissipation measure is a function of time alone, switched on only while the construction drains the solution to zero. | Active — read 2026-10-20 ([NOTE-1027](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1027.md)), skimmed, from arXiv:1710.11186v4: the introduction, Sections 2 and 3 (the dissipative Euler–Reynolds flow and the Main Lemma), Sections 4.1–4.5 (the shape of the construction, the coefficient equations and the energy increment), the opening of 4.10, Section 4.14, Section 5 and Section 6 in full were read; Sections 4.6–4.13, the estimates, were paged through and not checked.
