Read it knowing that "globally dissipative" means the local energy inequality (not whole-box dissipation, and not strict); that the exponent 1/15 is far below 1/3 (De Lellis and Kwon later reached 1/7 in Hölder spaces, Giri, Kwon and Novack 1/3 in L³-based ones); that the dissipation happens only in a short final interval in which the construction drains the solution to zero, its timing an input; that the shared initial datum is produced by the construction, not prescribed; that the "probabilistic method" is a binary choice per stage, not a random construction; and that the Burgers example of §1.2.1 misstates two constants (−d/dt∫u₀² is 1/3, not 2/3, and the threshold (1/6)^{1/3} is sufficient but not sharp, which is (1/4)^{1/3}), without affecting its point. |
| [LIT-1307](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1307.md) v2 | Data-driven model reduction, Wiener projections, and the Koopman-Mori-Zwanzig formalism | Lin & Lu (J. Comput. Phys. 2021). Writes data-driven model reduction for an invertible map with an invariant measure in Koopman-operator terms, derives the discrete Mori–Zwanzig equation from the Dyson formula, and introduces the Wiener projection: orthogonal projection onto the span of the entire past of chosen functions Ψ of the resolved variables. Under it the memory term vanishes, the reduced equation is the causal Wiener filter x_{n+1} = Σ_k Ψ(x_{n−k})h_k + ξ_{n+1}, and the residual is orthogonal to all of Ψ's past. A rational approximation of the filter's transfer function, called "uncontrolled" by the authors, turns it into a NARMAX-type recursion. | [LIT-1670](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1670.md) v2 | Long-Range Order in a Two-Dimensional Dynamical XY Model: How Birds Fly Together | Toner & Tu (1995), PRL 75. A continuum theory of a flock: a coarse-grained velocity field with a convective term, a preferred speed and noise, coupled to a conserved density. Its linearized theory loses order in d ≤ 2, as the equilibrium XY model does under the Mermin–Wagner theorem, but the convective nonlinearity is relevant below d = 4, and in d = 2 symmetry gives z = 6/5, ζ = 3/5, χ = −1/5, so the velocity fluctuations stay bounded and the flock has true long-range orientational order. The exactness rests on a cubic vertex staying irrelevant, which the authors "strongly suspect"; the order also follows from z < 2, expected "on physical grounds". | Active — read in full 2026-10-27 ([NOTE-1228](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1228.md)), from the arXiv preprint; worth reading as the founding hydrodynamic theory of flocking and as a clean case of order that an equilibrium system cannot have, stabilized by the coupling of order to transport. Its exponents are exact only on an argued-but-unproved step; its long-range order in two dimensions has a second, independent argument. |

A position paper by an 18-member network, two of whose authors led the Överkalix studies. It uses "transgenerational" for any outcome in offspring of an exposure in a parent before conception or in an earlier ancestor. In Överkalix cohorts of about 100 people each, a paternal grandfather's good food supply in mid-childhood went with higher mortality in his grandsons (rate ratio 1.67) and poor supply with lower (0.65); for paternal grandmothers and granddaughters, 2.13 and 0.72. They stay agnostic on mechanism and ask cohorts to collect ancestral exposure data. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1320](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1320.md)), in place of [LIT-1764](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1764.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as the Överkalix authors' own later account of their findings and of how they answer the charges of multiple testing and cultural confounding. |
| [LIT-1708](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1708.md) | Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance: a critical perspective | Bird (2024). A Perspective by a DNA-methylation biologist. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance rests on two assumptions: that the environment instructs the epigenome, and that acquired marks reach the germline and affect offspring. Both are weak in mammals. Marks usually follow transcription factors rather than lead; DNA methylation is largely stripped from gametes and early embryos; no validated mechanism links environment to epigenome. Organisms work to erase marks (mice inherit them when Dppa2 is mutated). The Agouti diet effect did not replicate. The rodent effects are short-lived or unreplicated, and the one robust paternal effect (microbiome ablation) seems not to go through the sperm epigenome. The human claims are weak: the Swedish (Överkalix) study ignored cultural transmission, failed to replicate in a larger cohort, and risks multiple testing; the Holocaust FKBP5 study had 32 people. Human genetics keeps explaining conditions once put down to environment. The article does not separate inter- from transgenerational effects. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1264.md)) from the publisher's PDF (CC BY); worth reading as the most recent sceptical statement, and the only one of the three to name and dispute the human trauma claims. |

The authors call the evidence accumulating but preliminary: small samples, cross-sectional designs, unmeasured confounds, possible publication bias. They use "transgenerational" for any parent-to-child effect, in utero exposure included. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1310](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1310.md)), in place of [LIT-1692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1692.md), which could not be fetched here; worth reading as a brief, sympathetic account of the Holocaust FKBP5 study and the few human studies beside it, by authors not on that study (though Rutten has published with its second author, Daskalakis; ref. 13). |
| [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md) | Molecular insights into transgenerational non-genetic inheritance of acquired behaviours | Bohacek & Mansuy (2015). Reviews rodent evidence that acquired behaviours and stress responses are transmitted through the germline, by sperm RNAs, DNA methylation and chromatin, and what remains open in humans. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. The ETH Research Collection and the Zurich repository (ZORA) list it without a file, as they do Mansuy's other reviews of 2013–2017. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Jawaid and Mansuy 2019 ([LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md)). |
| [LIT-1745](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1745.md) | Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance: Myths and Mechanisms | Heard & Martienssen (2014). A review of the mechanisms of epigenetic inheritance (small RNA, RNA-directed DNA methylation, paramutation, histone modification) and of germline reprogramming. Transgenerational inheritance is well documented in plants and nematodes, mostly at transposons and transgenes, and is rarely induced by the environment and more rarely adaptive. In mammals two rounds of reprogramming, in the germline and in the early embryo, erase most marks; the few bona fide epialleles (Agouti viable yellow, Axin fused) sit at retrotransposons. Effects of an exposed pregnant female count as transgenerational only from F3, of an exposed male only from F2. Human evidence, mostly nutritional (the Dutch famine, the thrifty phenotype), is intergenerational and confounded, so "so far there is little support"; human culture is the inheritance that is Lamarckian. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1254](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1254.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript (PMC4020004), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the standard map of epigenetic inheritance across plants, worms and mammals, and as the source of the F2/F3 rule the human trauma claims are measured against. |
| [LIT-1746](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1746.md) | Parental olfactory experience influences behavior and neural structure in subsequent generations | Dias & Ressler (2014). Male mice fear-conditioned to acetophenone or propanol before mating sired offspring (F1) and grand-offspring (F2) with heightened startle to, and lower detection thresholds for, the odour their F0 father was conditioned to, and not the other one. The offspring of acetophenone-trained males also had more M71 (Olfr151-expressing) olfactory neurons and larger M71 glomeruli; the anatomy, but not behaviour, was also tested and replicated in offspring conceived by IVF and carried by surrogates. Conditioning mothers before mating gave the same behavioural and anatomical effects, which survived cross-fostering. Olfr151 was less methylated in the sperm of conditioned F0 males (n = 12 vs 10) and of their naive F1 sons (n = 4 vs 4), but not in F1 or F2 olfactory epithelium. The authors read the effect as inherited sensitivity to a salient cue, not inherited fear, and leave open how an odour reaches sperm. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1281](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1281.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript (PMC3923835), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the standard animal case for germline transmission of a parent's experience: a specific, double-dissociated effect with IVF and cross-fostering controls, small groups, and a methylation result that is modest, confined to sperm and of unclear unit of analysis. This NOTE does not assess the later critique of the paper. |
| [LIT-1751](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1751.md) | Persistent epigenetic differences associated with prenatal exposure to famine in humans | Heijmans et al. (2008). Sixty people conceived during the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 had, about six decades later, less methylation in blood at the imprinted IGF2 gene's differentially methylated region than their unexposed same-sex siblings (0.488 vs 0.515, −5.2%, P = 5.9 × 10⁻⁵). Sixty-two people exposed only late in gestation, who were born lighter, showed no difference, and the timing interaction was significant. The authors read this as the first human evidence that a transient early-gestation exposure can be recorded as a lasting epigenetic change. The exposure is the person's own, in or around conception, so this is an intergenerational effect, not inheritance across untouched generations. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1248](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1248.md)) from the paper as reprinted in chapter 3 of Tobi's 2013 Leiden thesis (hdl.handle.net/1887/22065, Open Access); worth reading as the first human report of a prenatal exposure associated with a methylation difference decades later, and as the record's clearest case of the womb route: a mark from the person's own exposure, at the very start of gestation, with no claim about the next generation. |
| [LIT-1762](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1762.md) | A critical view on transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans | Horsthemke (2018). A Comment. Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance is documented in plants, nematodes and fruit flies; in mammals it must pass the Weismann barrier and two waves of reprogramming. Rodent reports mostly await independent confirmation, and the human ones (grandparental food supply, a Prader–Willi imprint) rest on unique cohorts. The Dutch Hunger Winter shows fetal programming, not germline transmission. Familial epimutations usually turn out to be secondary to a genetic variant. A proof needs: genetic, ecological and cultural inheritance excluded (F3 after an exposed pregnant female, F2 after an exposed male, with IVF and fostering); the factor found in pure germ cells; and the factor shown to cause the effect. In humans only genetic effects can be excluded. Cultural transmission very likely outweighs any epigenetic inheritance; the author remains sceptical. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1265](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1265.md)) from the published text (PMC6065375, CC BY), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service; worth reading as the shortest statement of what would prove germline epigenetic inheritance in humans, and of why the proof may be out of reach. |
| [LIT-1764](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1764.md) | Sex-specific, male-line transgenerational responses in humans | Pembrey et al. (2006). In historical records from Överkalix, Sweden, the food supply of paternal grandfathers in mid-childhood was associated with their grandsons' mortality, and that of paternal grandmothers with their granddaughters'. In the ALSPAC cohort, fathers who smoked early had sons with higher body mass. The authors propose sex-specific male-line transmission. | Unfetched — filed 2026-10-29, not read; set Unfetched the same day under [ADR-053](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-053.md): Nature marks the article free to read (nature.com/articles/5201538), but on 2026-10-29 the page served no body text and the PDF link redirected through Nature's sign-in back to the article page; it is not in PMC, and Unpaywall's submitted version is the abstract page. A human reader can likely open it. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unfetched until it is read, not on merit. Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Pembrey, Saffery and Bygren 2014 (LIT-1704). |
| [LIT-1774](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1774.md) | Inter- and transgenerational inheritance of behavioral phenotypes | Jawaid & Mansuy (2019). A short review from Mansuy's laboratory, the proponents' side. Rodent studies show that parental trauma, stress, drugs and in-utero insults pass behavioural phenotypes to offspring, in some models to the third or fourth generation, and that parental environmental enrichment passes benefits, and can prevent the transmission of trauma's effects. Germline dependence is shown by IVF and by injecting sperm RNA, which reproduces the phenotypes; non-coding RNAs are the best candidate carriers. Human studies of genocide survivors' descendants are offered as similar, and the review itself tables them as intergenerational. How a stimulus reaches the germline, and how effects pass beyond the first generation, are unknown. Germline reprogramming and the sceptics' objections are not discussed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1296](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1296.md)), in place of [LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the proponents' short statement of the rodent case for germline transmission of behaviour, read in place of Bohacek and Mansuy 2015 ([LIT-1738](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1738.md)), and for what it does not answer. |
| [LIT-1851](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1851.md) | Nonequilibrium phase transitions in coordinated biological motion: critical fluctuations | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner (1986), Physics Letters A 118(6):279–284. In bimanual wrist and finger movement paced to rising frequency, the standard deviation of relative phase grows as the anti-phase pattern nears its switch to in-phase and peaks in the transition, while the in-phase pattern shows neither growth nor a switch: the critical fluctuations HKB's stochastic extension predicts. Critical slowing is predicted, backed only by "very preliminary" spectral evidence, and left to later experiments. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1433.md)) in full, from an offprint scan posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/Kelso_1986_PhysLettersA.pdf), read from the page images; worth reading as the first quantified report of critical fluctuations in human coordination: the standard deviation of relative phase rises before the anti-phase to in-phase switch and peaks in it, in wrist and finger experiments, with no such rise when the same movement starts in-phase. Read it knowing that its figures average a few subjects or show one representative subject, that it gives no statistical test, and that critical slowing and hysteresis are not measured in it. |
| [LIT-1861](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1861.md) | Can populations be healthy? Perspectives from Georges Canguilhem and Geoffrey Rose | Giroux (2021), HPLS 43:111. Canguilhem held that health and disease apply only to individuals taken as organic totalities, because normativity, the capacity to institute new norms, is anchored in the organism; at the population level he preferred "hygiene" or "salubrity". Giroux argues that debates over units of selection and biological individuality loosen his link between individuality and organism, and that social epidemiology (Rose's causes of incidence, integral variables such as herd immunity and social capital, multilevel models) gives reasons for a concept of population health not reducible to individual health, while denying populations the ontological unity of an organism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1452](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1452.md)), from the published article in PubMed Central (PMC8527978; made available in the PMC Open Access Subset under Springer Nature's COVID-19 terms), fetched as XML through the Europe PMC REST API. Worth reading for two things. It argues, from social epidemiology (Rose's population causes, herd immunity, integral variables), that some health properties belong to populations and not to their members, against Canguilhem's restriction of health to the individual organism. And it quotes Canguilhem's definition of health as normativity in his own (translated) words: "the possibility of tolerating infractions of the habitual norm and instituting new norms in new situations" (The Normal and the Pathological, 1991, pp. 196–197). The Canguilhem it reports is at second hand. |
| [LIT-1873](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1873.md) | Dynamics governs switching among patterns of coordination in biological movement | Kelso, Scholz & Schöner (1988), Physics Letters A 134(1):8–12. When people switch on cue between in-phase and anti-phase finger movement, the switch from in-phase to anti-phase takes about twice as long as the reverse (four subjects, each p < 0.0001), with a longer-tailed distribution. Adding to the stochastic HKB equation a term that pulls relative phase toward the intended pattern reproduces the asymmetry and the distributions' shapes: intention acts within the pattern dynamics, not over them. | Active — read 2026-10-30 ([NOTE-1449](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1449.md)) in full, from the publisher's PDF posted on Kelso's lab page at Florida Atlantic University (https://ccs.fau.edu/hbblab/pdfs/1988_Kelso_Scholz_Schoner_Dynamics_governs_switching_among_pattern.pdf); worth reading as the experiment showing that an intended switch between bimanual patterns is shaped by their stability: switching from in-phase to anti-phase takes about twice as long as the reverse, with a longer tail, as the HKB dynamics with an added intentional term predicts. Read it knowing that it has four subjects, that the model's one new parameter was set to match the order of magnitude of the switching times, and that the critical slowing it mentions is cited from an earlier paper, not shown. |
| [LIT-1885](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1885.md) v2 | Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation for Biomolecular Processes | Barato & Seifert (2015). In a nonequilibrium steady state of a Markov jump network obeying local detailed balance, the entropy produced while a current is counted times the current's squared relative uncertainty is at least 2k_BT, independent of time. Proved within linear response for any network and for unicyclic networks at any affinity, where the sharper bound is (A/N) coth(A/2N), which also tightens the Fano-factor bound on the number of states in an enzyme cycle. For multicyclic networks far from equilibrium it is a conjecture supported by numerics on seven networks. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1480](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1480.md)); worth reading as the letter that named the thermodynamic uncertainty relation: a current counted in a steady state with relative uncertainty ε costs at least 2k_BT/ε² of dissipation, proved within linear response and for single-cycle networks, conjectured with numerical support for many-cycle ones ([THEORY-1268](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1268.md)). It bounds the precision of currents, not of occupations. |
| [LIT-1890](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1890.md) v2 | Stochastic dynamics and non-equilibrium thermodynamics of a bistable chemical system: the Schlögl model revisited | Vellela & Qian (2009). The Schlögl model A + 2X ⇌ 3X, B ⇌ X by rate equation, chemical master equation and open-system thermodynamics. Bistability requires the two chemostats out of equilibrium. The master equation has one two-peaked stationary distribution, so the long-run occupancy of the two states is set by parameters and volume, not by the initial condition, and which state dominates can change with volume alone. The slow eigenvalue, exponentially small in volume, is the sum of the two escape rates. The more stable state can carry the higher or the lower entropy production, and the Fokker–Planck approximation can pick the wrong dominant state. | Active — read in full 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1474](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1474.md)) from the PMC copy; worth reading as the clearest worked case of a maintained chemical state that is metastable at finite size: bistability needs the chemostats out of equilibrium, long-run occupancy does not depend on the starting state, the slow eigenvalue is the sum of the escape rates ([THEORY-1273](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1273.md)), and entropy production does not pick the stable state ([THEORY-1270](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1270.md)). Its large-volume rate formula carries a spurious 1/V, so its reported breakdown of asymptotics is mostly that factor. |
| [LIT-1892](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1892.md) v2 | Macroscopic stochastic thermodynamics | Falasco & Esposito (2025). Takes stochastic thermodynamics of jump processes with local detailed balance to a large-size limit. Extensive rates and potentials give a deterministic dynamics whose Lyapunov function is the quasi-potential, and a large-deviation theory of fluctuations that keeps the fluctuation theorem. Equilibrium, linear irreversible and Onsager–Machlup theories are recovered as limits. Transition rates between attractors go as e^{−VΔI} and are bracketed by the entropy produced along relaxation and escape paths, tightly only near detailed balance. Each attractor has a housekeeping dissipation, and Langevin approximations miss it and misjudge barriers. Minimum and maximum entropy production principles hold only in special regimes. | Active — read in part 2026-10-31 ([NOTE-1472](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1472.md), Skimmed: §§I–III, IV.A–D, IV.G–H, VI, VII.A.1, VIII and appendix A read in full; field theory and two of three applications not read); worth reading as the systematic statement of how maintained nonequilibrium states behave at large size: a quasi-potential, not a free energy, sets their lifetimes, which dissipation along relaxation and escape paths brackets ([THEORY-1264](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1264.md)); each carries its own housekeeping dissipation; and Gaussian-noise Langevin models get both barriers and entropy production wrong ([THEORY-1265](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1265.md)). |
| [LIT-1940](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1940.md) | Ecological scaffolding and the evolution of individuality | Black, Bourrat & Rainey (2020), DOI-10.1038/s41559-019-1086-9. A model in which an ecological scaffold, patchy resources with a regime of dispersal, imposes Darwinian properties on collectives of cells before any collective-level mechanism exists, so that selection can act on collectives from the start. Unread here; described from [LIT-188](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-188.md) §2 and the record's Bourrat readings. | Deferred — filed 2026-11-01, not read. Registered as the model Bourrat's endogenization account and Griesemer and Shavit's §2 ([LIT-188](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-188.md)) rest on. No reading was attempted. |
| [LIT-1956](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1956.md) v2 | Early-warning signals for critical transitions | Scheffer et al. (2009), Nature 461. A review of generic early-warning signals for critical transitions. Near a fold bifurcation the dominant eigenvalue goes to zero, so recovery from perturbations slows; under ongoing perturbation this shows as rising lag-1 autocorrelation and variance. Skewness and flickering are further signals. Spatial systems add rising cross-correlation and pattern sequences. Climate, ecosystem, epilepsy, asthma and finance cases are reviewed. The same signals, weaker, precede non-catastrophic thresholds; the timing of a shift stays hard to predict; cyclic and chaotic systems are "less well studied". | Active — read 2026-11-03 ([NOTE-1536](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1536.md), Skimmed), from the version reprinted as chapter 2 of Dakos's 2011 Wageningen thesis (edepot.wur.nl/168815), its two technical boxes not extractable; worth reading as the standard review of generic early warnings of tipping points, critical slowing down above all, and for its own caution that the same signals precede non-catastrophic thresholds. |
| [LIT-1958](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1958.md) | Integrals of motion as slow modes in dissipative many-body operator dynamics | Yang & Abanin (2025), PRB 112, 094304. Under weak local noise an operator's norm decays at a rate proportional to its size, the number of sites it acts on. Under chaotic Hamiltonian dynamics generic operators grow, so they decay ever faster, while small-sized integrals of motion do not grow and decay slowly. Exact diagonalization of the Lindbladian for Ising and Heisenberg chains of up to nine sites finds the slowest eigenoperators to be linear combinations of the known exact and approximate integrals of motion, and turns up approximate ones not put in by hand. A perturbation theory argues that this survives at large size because the relevant gap is not the level spacing but one of order min(γL, √(v_Bγ)); the authors add that hydrodynamic modes may close that gap. | Active — read in full 2026-11-02 ([NOTE-1534](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1534.md)), from arXiv:2506.02970v3 with its supplementary material; worth reading as a clean physical case of slowness picking out structure: under weak local noise, a Hamiltonian's small conserved quantities are the slowest modes because they do not spread, while generic operators spread and decay. The correspondence is shown by exact diagonalization at nine sites or fewer; its large-system footing is a perturbative argument the authors qualify themselves. |
| [LIT-2021](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2021.md) | Branches of Triangulated Origami Near the Unfolded State | Chen & Santangelo (2018). A flat triangulated rigid origami is a singular point of its configuration space: at first order every vertical displacement is a motion, so linearization fails. Expanding the length constraints to second order, each self stress of the flat network gives one quadratic constraint on vertex heights, and the wheel stress at each internal vertex is exactly preservation of its zero Gaussian curvature, so a single vertex's near-flat configurations form a double cone, popped up or popped down. For patterns with four boundary vertices, numerical root-finding on random triangulations finds 2^Vi branches meeting at the flat state, two per vertex sign pattern up to global sign, proven for H1 triangulations. The authors infer that a sheet folded from flat is likely to misfold, and that driving forces orthogonal to every wrong branch cannot be found for even modest Vi. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1614](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1614.md)) from the arXiv v2 author version, main text in full and appendices skimmed; worth reading as the second-order rigidity theory of flat triangulated rigid origami: each self stress of the flat sheet gives a quadratic constraint on vertex heights, the wheel stress at an internal vertex is exactly preservation of zero Gaussian curvature there, and the flat state is a singular point where, in every triangulation computed, 2^Vi branches meet, two for each pattern of vertex popping states up to global sign. Its main limits: the count is numerical except for the rare H1 triangulations, second-order solutions are not proven to be configurations, only four-boundary-vertex (one degree of freedom) patterns are treated, and the analysis is local to the flat state and purely kinematic. |
| [LIT-2024](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2024.md) | Topological transitions in the configuration space of non-Euclidean origami | Berry, Lee-Trimble & Santangelo (2020). In origami with flat faces and curvature K = 2π − Σα at the vertices, the second-order isometry condition at a vertex becomes hᵀQh = K, with Q having one negative eigenvalue. Near the flat state, for small K and fold angles kept in (−π, π), a vertex with K > 0 has a two-sheeted solution set whose popped-up and popped-down nappes are disconnected, and one with K < 0 a one-sheeted set joining them by a neck; numerical tracing of a 5-fold vertex agrees, and degree-4 vertices are disconnected for both signs. Under an assumption, multi-vertex branches distinguished by a K > 0 vertex's nappe are disconnected too. The authors propose curvature as a handle against misfolding. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1605](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1605.md)) from the arXiv v1 preprint; worth reading as the extension of second-order origami rigidity to vertices carrying Gaussian curvature, and for the finding that the sign of the curvature changes the topology of the near-flat configuration space: a non-intersecting vertex with positive curvature has its popped-up and popped-down nappes split into disconnected components, one with negative curvature keeps them joined by a neck, and a degree-4 vertex is split for either sign. Its main limits: local to the flat state and small curvature; the disconnection depends on forbidding self-intersection; the multi-vertex statement rests on an assumption and leaves open which combinations of nappes exist; the published PRE text was not compared. |
| [LIT-2025](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2025.md) | Reconfigurable origami-based metamaterials with a transition between compact flat-foldable and load-bearing states | Rahardjo, Navaratnam & Zhang (2026). Unverified until read: no copy and no abstract were reached, and the identification with the work the pasted synthesis on constraint architectures meant is fair confidence, not confirmed. By its title, it concerns reconfigurable origami-based metamaterials that move between a compact flat-foldable state and a load-bearing one. The synthesis describes it as a study of the trade-off between flat-foldability and load-bearing capacity. | Unfetched — not read; the article, open access under CC BY 4.0 per Crossref, located but not fetched on 2026-11-05. The ScienceDirect article page, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0093641326000686, returned HTTP 403; not retried. The Elsevier API text link Crossref gives, https://api.elsevier.com/content/article/PII:S0093641326000686?httpAccept=text/plain, returned HTTP 400 (the API needs a key). No abstract was available from Crossref. Its identification as the work the pasted synthesis meant is fair confidence, not confirmed. No neighbour was read. |
| [LIT-2026](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2026.md) | Cellular Automata Inspired Multistable Origami Metamaterials for Mechanical Learning | Liu, Fang, Xu & Wang (2023). A stacked Miura-origami metamaterial whose bistable cells evolve under a prescribed sequence of tension and compression is used as the reservoir of a reservoir computer: inputs are written as an initial configuration, the actuation drives snap-through transitions, and a trained linear readout classifies from the visited configurations. A 4×2-cell prototype recognizes ten 5×4-pixel digits and noisy versions in experiment; in simulation, binarized MNIST reaches 90.4% against 87.2% without the reservoir, and a retained buffer of cells carries history on a 5-bit memory task. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1600](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1600.md)) from the published version's full text in Europe PMC (CC BY 4.0) and the arXiv preprint, Supporting Information skipped; worth reading as a reservoir computer whose reservoir is a multistable origami metamaterial, and for the plain finding that a bad actuation rule erases its inputs. Its main limits: the learning is in a trained linear readout, not in the material; only the small-digit task (ten 5×4-pixel digits on a 4×2-cell prototype) was done in experiment, MNIST and the memory task in simulation; the gain over the raw inputs on MNIST is modest (87.2% to 90.4%); the publisher's table-of-contents text overstates what was done in experiment. |
| [LIT-2029](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2029.md) | Synthesis of Bistable Compliant Structures from Truss Mechanisms | Kinoshita & Ohsaki (2009). Bistable compliant mechanisms are easier to find as pin-jointed trusses, since optimizing frames with geometric nonlinearity failed to converge because of local buckling, but a pin- jointed truss cannot be made in one piece. The authors convert a given bistable truss, whose second stable state is snap-through held by contact with an obstacle, into an equivalent frame: each pin joint becomes a pseudo-joint of thin end regions whose area and length ratios are optimized to keep the output displacement and a second self-equilibrium state, under a cap on strain that stops deformation lumping into a point hinge. A two-bar study and one seven-node example show it. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1597](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1597.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF on J-STAGE; worth reading as a short worked case of a design found in one constraint model (pin-jointed bars, no bending) having to be re-realized in another (rigid joints with bending) by a second optimization: a bistable truss mechanism, whose second stable state is snap-through stopped by an obstacle, is converted into a single-piece frame by sizing thin end regions at the former pin joints under a strain cap, so that no point hinge forms. Its main limits: one numerical example, no fabrication or experiment, equivalence shown only by overlaid force–displacement curves, and the second stable state still rests on a placed obstacle. |
| [LIT-2030](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2030.md) | General-purpose mechanical computing enabled by origami circuit reconfiguration with robotic addressing and activation | Chen, Tan & Yan (2025). A bistable Kresling unit with a magnetic cap snaps between states under an in-plane magnetic torque and keeps its state with the field removed; right- and left-handed units are Buffer and NOT switches, one unit can carry several switches, and a logic-synthesis method minimizes the units needed. A "mechanical programmable gate array" lays out one module per minterm; a wheeled robot steered by the outputs of two origami units follows a field of magnets and sets the modules it passes, which programs the function. Demonstrations include full adder and subtractor, a 2-bit adder or multiplier, and a mobile full adder that reuses itself. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1559](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1559.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), main text in full, most of Methods and all Supplementary Notes skipped; worth reading as an engineered case of memory held in configuration (non-volatile bistable switches) and of programmability moved from wiring into an addressing path. Its main limits: general-purpose only over pre-built minterm modules, whose number grows as 2^n per output; programming needs a designed layout of magnets and a robot with motors and power, and outputs are read as voltages; the neural-network weight update is described, not shown in the main text; no error rates for whole arrays. |
| [LIT-2031](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2031.md) v2 | Design of Parallel Flexure Systems via Freedom and Constraint Topologies (FACT) | Hopkins (2007), MIT S.M. thesis, supervised by Culpepper. A rigid stage is tied to ground in parallel by flexures idealised as constraints stiff along their axes and infinitely compliant across them. Motions are twists, constraints wrenches; a twist is permitted when it does no work against every constraint wrench, so the freedom space is the null space of the wrench matrix. Each freedom space is drawn as a geometric figure linked one to one with a constraint space ("the Principle of Complementary Topologies"), and for pure-force constraints the pairs fall into 26 types in six cases by the number of non-redundant constraints. A six-step procedure goes from the desired motions to the constraints, and then adds redundant constraints for stiffness, symmetry and load capacity without changing the kinematics. | Active — read 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1592](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1592.md)), all but the case-by-case derivations and appendices, from the scanned thesis in DSpace@MIT; worth reading as the origin of Freedom and Constraint Topologies (FACT), the screw-theoretic design method for parallel flexures in which a stage's permitted motions (its freedom space) and the lines along which constraints can be added without changing them (its constraint space) determine each other, and for its kinematic definition of a redundant constraint: one whose addition or removal leaves the freedom space unchanged while stiffness, load capacity and stability change. Its main limits: the 26 freedom/constraint pairs it catalogues hold only for ideal pure-force constraints under small motions (the thesis itself finds more types once general wrenches are allowed), it covers parallel systems only, and it leaves out elastomechanics, dynamics and actuation. A master's thesis, not peer reviewed. |
| [LIT-2034](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2034.md) | Laser reprogramming magnetic anisotropy in soft composites for reconfigurable 3D shaping | Deng, Sattari, Xie, Liao, Yan & Lin (2020). A silicone film holds NdFeB microparticles encapsulated in polycaprolactone, which melts at about 60 °C. A laser scanned over chosen regions melts the polymer locally; the freed particles align with a programming magnetic field and are fixed as it resolidifies. Writing different directions into different regions encodes a magnetization pattern that, under one uniform 150 mT actuation field, bends the film into a designed 3D shape, and the pattern can be erased and rewritten the same way. Shown: strips folding along domain boundaries that act as creases, origami-like shapes, a multistate switch and kirigami robots whose gait changes with the written pattern; shapes held over 100 cycles with alternating reprogramming. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1565](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1565.md)) from the NSF Public Access Repository copy of the published article (CC BY 4.0); worth reading as a concrete case of a frozen configuration made rewritable by a phase change: a silicone film whose magnetic particles sit in a meltable polymer has its magnetization pattern rewritten by local laser melting under a programming field and fixed again on cooling, so one film gives many shapes under the same actuation field. Registered as a neighbour standing in for Yeow, Yang and Ren (2024), [LIT-2113](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2113.md), on the phase-change half of its idea only. | [LIT-2041](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2041.md) | Energetic rigidity. I. A unifying theory of mechanical stability | Damavandi, Hagh, Santangelo & Manning (2022; arXiv 2021). The paper separates energetic rigidity, in which every nontrivial global motion raises the energy, from structural rigidity, in which no such motion preserves the constraints; for Hookean energies they coincide when the system is unstressed and can differ under prestress. It classifies when the cheap tests imply energetic rigidity: with no states of self-stress, first-order rigidity (constraint counting) suffices; with them, the spectrum of the prestress matrix decides, second-order rigidity sufficing when it is zero or positive semidefinite, and no general result holding when it has negative eigenvalues. It argues that energetic rigidity is the more useful notion in practice, and that dynamics and external tension drive systems to the non-generic configurations, with self-stresses, where counting fails. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1570](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1570.md)) from the arXiv v2 PDF; worth reading as a single classification of when the geometric rigidity tests (first-order rigidity, that is constraint counting, second-order rigidity, the shear modulus) imply energetic rigidity, in which every nontrivial motion raises the energy: counting suffices only without states of self-stress, and with them the prestress matrix's spectrum decides. Also for its points that dynamics and forcing drive systems to the non-generic configurations where counting fails, and that the prestress a system adopts need not be the one that stabilizes it. Its main limits: Hookean energies quadratic in the constraints only; no analytic result when the prestress matrix has negative eigenvalues; the applications are in a companion paper II, not read. |
| [LIT-2042](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2042.md) v2 | Design of Flexure-based Motion Stages for Mechatronic Systems via Freedom, Actuation and Constraint Topologies (FACT) | Hopkins (2010), MIT Ph.D. thesis, supervised by Culpepper. Extends FACT in two directions. Allowing twists and wrenches of every pitch gives 50 freedom/constraint space types; only those inside a "parallel pyramid" can be built from parallel flexures, and the rest, such as three pure translations, need parallel modules stacked in series, whose intermediate freedom spaces add up and, when they exceed the system's freedoms, leave it underconstrained, with poor dynamics. A twist–wrench stiffness matrix maps a motion to the wrench that produces it; the resulting actuation space, of which there are 26 types, says where a minimal set of linear actuators must act to drive the freedoms without parasitic error. One bench stage found the least error with the actuator about 17.5 cm below the probe tip, against 20 cm predicted. | Active — read 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1596](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1596.md)), all but the type-by-type catalogue and most of the appendices, from the DSpace@MIT scan and the born-digital copy on the author's UCLA lab site; worth reading as the extension of FACT to serial flexures and to actuation: a chart of 50 freedom/constraint space types once constraints of any pitch are allowed, a "parallel pyramid" bounding what parallel flexures can realise (three pure translations need modules stacked in series), underconstraint as freedoms left in intermediate bodies, and an actuation space, computed from the flexures' stiffness, along which linear actuators must act to drive the permitted motions without parasitic error. Its main limits: small motions and quasi-static actuation, parallel systems only for actuation, a single bench experiment whose errors were much larger than predicted, and a 50-type completeness resting on an appendix and the master's thesis. In disordered central-force spring networks derived from jammed packings, a chosen linear strain ratio η between a target pair of nodes and a distant source pair is tuned in by removing bonds one at a time, each chosen by an analytic update computed from the network's states of self-stress and of compatible stress without re-solving it. About 1% of the bonds in 2D and 0.5% in 3D suffice for η = ±1, failing in under 2% and 1% of networks; one source can drive several targets, and several independent pairs can be tuned at once. Laser-cut and 3D-printed networks reproduce the responses. A quad kirigami sheet of L × L rigid squares is read as a linkage: each uncut hinge is a link pinning two corners, and degrees of freedom (DoF) come from the rank of a rigidity matrix. Each degree-N origami vertex has N − 3 internal degrees of freedom, solved by spherical trigonometry, whose solutions are "generically multi-valued", giving several configuration branches. (2014), [LIT-2044](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2044.md); worth reading as a lattice theory of origami tessellations in which each degree-N vertex has N − 3 internal degrees of freedom with several configuration branches, and in which the Miura-ori, with facet bending modelled as extra folds, has soft modes localized at its edges with an analytic decay length, checked on a paper sheet with reversible pop-through defects, so that its degrees of freedom scale with the perimeter. Bistable Kresling "barrels" folded from mylar are bits; four of different pattern angle, stacked in series with ends clamped against rotation, form a Preisach system whose 16 states are all stable and reachable by a prescribed sequence of compression and extension, with return-point memory. | [LIT-2074](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2074.md) | The Complexity of Folding Self-Folding Origami | Stern, Pinson & Murugan (2017), read from the arXiv v1 preprint. A generic 4-vertex has two folding branches meeting at the flat state. Around a loop of vertices three can choose freely and the fourth is over-determined, so most global branch choices have energy of order κρ⁴: a glassy landscape whose number of distractor branches grows as 2^(α√A), exponentially in the sheet's boundary length, even when the designed branch is the ground state. Folding is zero-temperature descent from the flat state, so randomly placed actuators usually land in a distractor; on one 4 × 4 pattern 18 of 60 creases had to be actuated for a 50% chance. The union of the actuated creases' "folding islands" predicts success better than their number, and an extra actuator can ruin a successful folding. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1571](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1571.md)) from the arXiv v1 preprint, 1703.04161v1, titled "The difficulty of folding self-folding origami"; the published PRX version was not read. Worth reading as the case in which a target configuration exists and is designed to be the ground state, yet is hard to reach: a crease pattern with one designed folding motion still has exponentially many dead-end "distractor" branches at the flat state, from frustrated loops of two-branch vertices, so random actuation usually misfolds, and whether the actuated creases' "folding islands" cover the sheet predicts success better than how many creases are actuated. | [LIT-2078](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2078.md) | Topological boundary modes in isostatic lattices | Kane & Lubensky (2014; arXiv 2013). The dynamical matrix of a ball-and-spring frame is QQᵀ, Q the equilibrium matrix; its "square root" has the symmetries of a topological band class, so gapped isostatic lattices are classified by winding numbers of det Q(k). A local index theorem follows: the zero-mode count in a region is a local count of sites and bonds, the classical Maxwell term, plus a topological count fixed by the bulk's topological polarization at the region's boundary. So zero modes can arise where there is no local mismatch of constraints and freedoms. A 1D rotor chain mapping onto the SSH model and a deformed kagome lattice show end, edge and domain-wall modes: floppy modes on walls of one orientation, states of self-stress on the other. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1601](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1601.md)) from the arXiv v2 PDF, main text and supplementary proof; worth reading as the paper that connects isostatic mechanics to topological band theory: a local index theorem in which the zero-mode count of a region is a local count of sites and bonds plus a topological count fixed by winding numbers of the bulk equilibrium matrix, so that floppy modes, and states of self-stress, can sit at boundaries and domain walls where constraints and degrees of freedom locally balance. Its main limits: linear, harmonic theory, silent on whether the zero modes extend to finite mechanisms; a bulk gap and a gauge choice of unit cell are required; only 1D and 2D models are worked; the boundary modes themselves were found earlier, by Sun et al. |
| [LIT-2080](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2080.md) v2 | Second-Order Rigidity and Prestress Stability for Tensegrity Frameworks | Connelly & Whiteley (1996). For tensegrity frameworks, of bars, cables that may not lengthen and struts that may not shorten, the paper defines prestress stability and second-order rigidity and proves that first-order rigidity implies prestress stability, which implies second-order rigidity, which implies rigidity, with examples that none of the implications reverses, even for bar frameworks. A duality, the second-order stress test, decides whether a first-order flex extends to second order from the framework's proper self-stresses; when either the cone of flexes or the cone of proper self-stresses is one-dimensional, second-order rigidity and prestress stability coincide. As an application it proves Roth's conjecture on convex polygons with interior cables. | Active — read 2026-11-05 and 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1588](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1588.md)) from the scanned published version posted on the first author's Cornell publications page: everything but the applications of §§5.4–5.6 and Appendix A.2–A.3, proofs included. Worth reading as the rigorous placing of prestress stability, borrowed from structural engineering, between first-order rigidity and second-order rigidity for frameworks with bars, cables and struts, with examples that no step of the hierarchy reverses, and a second-order stress test, a Farkas alternative pairing first-order flexes with proper self-stresses. Its main limits: local rigidity only, global rigidity being a different notion; testing second-order rigidity is hard in general; the flex-extension result is proved only for independent bar frameworks and only to second order. |
| [LIT-2081](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2081.md) | Mechanism of DNA origami folding elucidated by mesoscopic simulations | DeLuca, Duke, Ye, Poirier, Ke, Castro & Arya (2024). A bead model of DNA (8 nucleotides per bead) with a force field that switches with hybridization state simulates full isothermal folding of square-lattice origami up to 8192 nucleotides. A four-helix bundle folds hierarchically: staples bridge the scaffold, a cooperative zipping collapses it into a swollen, globally disordered precursor, and global order then grows slowly. Scaffold routing and long staples change the pathway. A 32-helix bundle folds slowly and variably, and some runs end with unfolded interiors in global topological traps that early progress did not predict. Simulation only. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1561](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1561.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY 4.0), main text in full, later Methods and Supplementary Information skipped; worth reading as a coarse-grained model that reaches the whole folding timescale of DNA origami while keeping configuration, and for its argument that hybridization-state kinetic models can overpredict yield. A flat-foldable origami cell carrying conductors is a switch that conducts when folded (Buffer) or when not (NOT); two in series make AND, in parallel OR, and rotating them inside a gate switches between the two without rewiring. Gates cascade through electromagnets. A 30-gate array is reconfigured among a 2-bit adder, subtractor, comparator and multiplier, and a Rubik's-cube arrangement of elements changes its function by layer rotations; a built third-order cube switches between full adder and full subtractor, and a second-order cube rotated by a servo serves as a wheeled robot's decision module. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1608](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1608.md)) from the publisher's open-access PDF (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), main text in full, most of Methods and all Supplementary Information skipped; worth reading as a clean engineered case in which the function a device computes, the arrangement that fixes the function, and the mechanism that changes the arrangement are separate parts. Conical Kresling origami is modelled as a truss of linear springs; a small network mapping height to twist is trained without data, by minimizing energy along the torque-free path, and jointly with the geometric parameters for inverse design from two stable heights and a barrier. Forward predictions match a beam-truss FEA (R² > 0.93) and inverse designs their targets (R² > 0.99). Its main limits: a truss model that omits crease rotation stiffness, bending, buckling, friction and contact; the "FEA validation" uses the same truss abstraction, so only the one three-layer prototype tests the mechanics, and there the absolute barriers differ from prediction and are compared after normalizing to the bottom layer; inverse design returns one of many geometries. |
| [LIT-2091](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2091.md) | Origami frustration and its influence on energy landscapes of origami assemblies | Zang, Zhao, Misseroni & Paulino (2025). A standard Kresling origami cell is bistable with an energy landscape fixed at fabrication. Springs added along the axis, about it, or along the mountain creases prestress the cell ("geometrical frustration", global or crease-level), move its first stable state to a nonzero base energy, tune its energy barrier continuously and can switch it from bistable to monostable. In a stack of three cells with 8 stable states and 56 ordered transitions, 16 need intermediate states and 8 more are blocked by the ordering of the cells' barriers, leaving 32 feasible; prestressing reorders the barriers in place and makes the 8 blocked transitions feasible. Also shown: frustration-dependent history effects under twist, a frustrated curved-crease tube, and a shape-morphing truss. | Active — main text read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1569](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1569.md)) from the full-text JATS XML in Europe PMC (PMC12435273, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0); worth reading as a clean case of mechanical frustration in the energetic sense: springs that prestress a bistable Kresling origami cell from outside, at the crease or the whole cell, tune its energy barrier continuously and can switch it to monostable, and in a three-cell stack reordering the barriers in place opens the eight of 56 transitions that the barrier ordering had blocked. Its main limits: three-cell assemblies, linear springs in the main analysis, a theory that misses the panel buckling seen in experiment, and a frustration supplied and adjusted by the designer, not by the structure. | [LIT-2099](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2099.md) | Hinge-Free Compliant Mechanism Design via the Topological Level-Set | Krishnakumar & Suresh (2015). Compliant-mechanism topology optimization must trade flexibility at the output against stiffness against a workpiece, and density-based (SIMP) designs tend to form point hinges. The authors maximize mutual strain energy over a weighted sum of input and output strain energies, the weight η trading geometric against mechanical advantage, and remove material where the topological derivative of that ratio is lowest, with fixed-point iterations at each volume fraction. Elements are in or out, so no pseudo-densities and no point hinges; one run gives designs of decreasing volume. Examples: 2D inverters, a cruncher, a grasper, a 3D inverter and flap. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1582](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1582.md)) from a manuscript posted on the second author's lab page at UW-Madison, most likely the authors' manuscript of the journal article; registered as a stand-in for Sigmund (1997), [LIT-2043](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2043.md), and more thinly for the review by Zhu et al. (2020), [LIT-2051](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2051.md). Worth reading as a compact statement of what compliant-mechanism topology optimization trades: flexibility at the output against stiffness against a workpiece, a multi-objective problem with Pareto solutions, and density-based designs that exploit the model with point hinges. Its own method removes material by the topological derivative of a mutual-to-weighted-input-and-output strain-energy ratio, avoiding pseudo-densities and hinges, with one parameter trading geometric against mechanical advantage. Its main limits: linear elasticity, coarse meshes, no springs or stress constraints, no fabrication, comparisons qualitative. |
| [LIT-2100](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2100.md) | Origami structures with a critical transition to bistability arising from hidden degrees of freedom | Silverberg, Na, Evans, Liu, Hull, Santangelo, Lang, Hayward & Cohen (2015). The square twist's crease pattern is isostatic: with rigid facets it admits only two isolated states, unfolded and folded, and "should not be foldable". Paper square twists fold by bending their facets along the short diagonals of the rhombi, a hidden degree of freedom separated from the crease DOF by an energy gap. Bending against crease stiffness gives a critical plane angle (≈25° for paper) below which the twist is monostable and above which it snaps bistably; simulations put the boundary at 10 < k_b/k_c < 100, and paper measures about 36. A sub-millimetre self-folding gel twist shows the hysteresis, and adding creases where bending would occur removes it. The thesis: the number of DOF changes with the energy scale probed. | Active — letter read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1554.md)), SI pp. 1–2 skimmed, from the published PDF posted by co-author Robert J. Lang on his publications page; worth reading as a minimal case in which the number of degrees of freedom depends on the energy scale probed: the square twist's crease pattern is isostatic and rigidly admits only its unfolded and folded states, yet paper square twists fold by bending their facets, and the ratio of bending to crease stiffness, with the plane angle, sets a critical transition between monostable and bistable folding. The classical Maxwell–Calladine count uses only the compatibility matrix and so ignores bond stiffness and prestress. Characterizing linear response by four susceptibilities, the authors derive a generalized index theorem, N_dof − N_c = #LZEFs − #ZDTs, that holds with nonzero prestress and heterogeneous stiffness. The zero-displacement tensions are the states of self-stress; the linear zero-extension forces map one-to-one onto the linear zero modes but in general span a different subspace. A creased thin sheet folds from flat into one of exponentially many structures depending on the applied force pattern, so it is a random classifier of force patterns. DNA origami joints in the manner of macroscopic machine design: stiff double-stranded bundles connected only by single-stranded scaffold make a slider and a hinge, each moving in one designed degree of freedom whose range and stiffness the connection lengths set. In the kinetic Tile Assembly Model, a mismatched tile on the growth front is often covered by further growth before it can detach, which forces a speed/error trade-off r ≈ βε²: ten times fewer errors cost a hundredfold slowdown. Replacing each tile by a K×K block whose internal edges carry unique labels keeps the logical assembly the same, scaled by K, but leaves no way to extend a single mismatch without a second error, so growth stalls and the bad tile falls off. In simulation 2×2 blocks give r ≈ βε, and at fixed conditions errors fall from 1% to 0.01%; the predicted gain exponential in K falls short at K = 3, which the authors attribute to growth on facets, which proofreading does not correct. Proofreading tiles also heal punctures, sometimes leaving "scar tissue". In origami, a staple's first domain pays the translational entropy and its later domains bind within one structure, but each loop closed with the scaffold constrains it at a cost that depends on the order of binding; in the small designs simulated a staple typically binds fully once started, assembly is mostly downhill and needs no nucleation barrier, and blocking is rare at typical concentrations. | [LIT-2163](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2163.md) | Factors affecting success of conservation translocations of terrestrial vertebrates: A global systematic review | Morris, Brook, Moseby & Johnson (2021), read as the 2021 preprint. A global database of 514 conservation translocations of terrestrial vertebrates (1895–2017), from Web of Science and the IUCN's "Global re-introduction perspectives" reports, modelled on two outcomes: categorical success calibrated to practitioners' own labels (n = 257) and generation-weighted population growth (n = 87). Success rises with numbers released up to about 20–50 individuals, then plateaus; Oceania does worse. Captive-bred and wild stock have similar reported success ("wild 70.2%, captive 76.0%"), but captive-bred stock has negative mean growth (−2.8 against +2.2) and captive sourcing is among the strongest predictors of growth; soft and hard release have similar reported success (79.8% against 75.0%), but hard release shows higher growth (+5.6 against −1.3). The authors read the captive gap as possible leniency "with success criteria" among practitioners invested in captive breeding. The outcome scale's top rung is a population "likely to persist without further augmentation", which only 24.8% of the IUCN successes reached. Raw group means with wide spreads, not adjusted contrasts. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1657](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1657.md)) as the authors' EcoEvoRxiv preprint, "Lessons from a century of conservation translocations" (doi:10.32942/osf.io/hnzqk, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0), not the published version, which could not be reached; any change between the two is unknown. Worth reading as the largest standardized global synthesis of terrestrial-vertebrate translocations (514, 1895–2017) and for showing that practitioner-judged success and population growth after release disagree: captive-bred stock and soft release match wild stock and hard release on reported success but show lower population growth. Its limits: source and release method are raw group means with large spreads in a growth subset of 87, not model-adjusted contrasts; success is self-reported and calibrated on a handful of questionnaire returns; reporting bias is strong (8% failures in the IUCN reports); the supplement and the coefficients' figures were not seen. |

Translocations of greater prairie chickens into Illinois in 1992–1998 made the population a textbook case of genetic rescue. A pedigree of 12,700 Hood River winter steelhead at eight microsatellite loci over 15 run-years tests two predictions that domestication selection makes and relaxed selection does not. Both hold. First-generation hatchery fish "had nearly double the lifetime reproductive success" of wild fish when both were spawned in the hatchery; and among wild broodstock, those most successful in the hatchery left offspring least successful in the wild (0.62 against 2.05 returning offspring), in 7 of 8 run-years. Inbreeding cannot explain it. The one exception, a release year with few broodstock, few smolts reared at low density and released larger, "points to crowding as a possible selection pressure". The authors conclude that less than one generation in captivity can produce "a rapid, genetically based fitness reduction in the wild". | Active — main text read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1652](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1652.md)) from the free full text on PMC (PMC3252900); the supplementary tables were not read. | [LIT-2192](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2192.md) | Fitness of hatchery-reared salmonids in the wild | Araki, Berejikian, Ford & Blouin (2008). A review of studies comparing hatchery and wild salmonids' fitness in the same natural habitat, with a quantitative-genetic model. Hatchery fish are generally less fit in the wild; nonlocal stocks kept closed for 5–10 generations worst (lifetime relative fitness 0.02–0.37); stocks from local wild broodstock "generally perform better than nonlocal stocks, but often worse than wild fish". For the authors' Hood River steelhead the decline is fast, inherited and cumulative from the first to the second hatchery generation. Of relaxed selection, inbreeding and domestication selection, the last is judged "The last and most likely explanation", and the model finds that it can give a decline of more than 30% per generation on one trait only under strong selection in both settings and high heritability, plausibly on several traits. Using local wild broodstock mitigates the loss "to some extent", and no rise in wild productivity from hatcheries is documented. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1668](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1668.md)) from the open-access Europe PMC full text of PMC3352433; worth reading as the same laboratory's review of hatchery against wild salmonid fitness in the wild, the stand-in for its Science paper of 2007 ([LIT-2159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2159.md)), whose relative-fitness estimates and design it reports, and for its model of when domestication selection can account for a loss of more than 30% per hatchery generation. Fourteen studies, mostly steelhead, with little power below a 10–15% difference; the model is one generation and, in its worked form, one trait; the mechanism is argued, not measured. |

| [LIT-2196](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2196.md) | Dissipative solitons for mode-locked lasers | Grelu & Akhmediev (2012). A review defining dissipative solitons against conservative ones and applying the idea to passively mode-locked lasers. A conservative soliton comes from a "single balance between nonlinearity and dispersion" and is one of "a family comprising an infinity of soliton solutions"; a dissipative soliton is "a fixed localised solution", an attractor whose energy, profile and chirp are "predetermined by the equation parameters, rather than by the initial conditions", kept by an exact gain–loss balance, a "continuous energy exchange with the environment" and an internal flow from regions that gain energy to regions that lose it. The master model is the cubic–quintic complex Ginzburg–Landau equation. It surveys pulse shapes, high-energy designs, robust soliton molecules, pulsating and exploding solitons, soliton rain nucleating from noise above a fluctuation threshold, and cavity solitons switched on and off by a transient writing beam. Theory, simulation and experiment surveyed; no new results. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1688](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1688.md)) from the authors' accepted manuscript on HAL (hal-04901011, CC BY 4.0), which carries revision marks and is not the typeset article; worth reading as a short statement, by two of the concept's main authors, of what separates a dissipative soliton from a conservative one: a single attractor fixed by the equation's parameters, held by an exact gain–loss balance with a continuous exchange and an internal flow of energy, rather than one member of a family selected by the initial data. Its main limits: it is a review of mode-locked lasers, with no new results; it gives no pump existence threshold and never discusses bistability or hysteresis; it says nothing on merger or annihilation; and its reach into biology is a citation only. |
| [LIT-2197](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2197.md) v2 | A review on radiation of oscillons and oscillatons | Fodor (2019). A review, from the author's D.Sc. thesis, of long-lived oscillating localized states of a real scalar field: oscillons on a fixed background and oscillatons when self-gravitating, mainly of the small but nonzero radiation they emit. Only the 1+1 sine-Gordon breather is exactly periodic (derived for one-parameter families shrinking to the vacuum; isolated breathers found "unlikely" numerically); every other oscillon radiates, at a rate exponentially small in the amplitude parameter, computed by spectral numerics or by complex extension, asymptotic matching and Borel summation. Oscillons form from generic initial data. Stability follows from whether energy rises with central amplitude; 3+1 dimensional oscillons are stable only above a minimum amplitude and, carried below it by radiation, suddenly decay after a few thousand oscillations, while small and moderate lower-dimensional ones never decay. The author's independent code reproduces the Gaussian-data results of Gleiser and of Copeland, Gleiser & Müller. | Active — read 2026-11-06, Chapter 2 in full ([NOTE-1698](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1698.md)) from arXiv:1911.03340v1, as a neighbour of Copeland, Gleiser & Müller (1995), [LIT-2200](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2200.md); worth reading as the long later account of why oscillons end: on its account, apart from the 1+1 sine-Gordon breather no real-scalar oscillon is exactly periodic, all radiate at a rate exponentially small in their amplitude parameter but nonzero, and in 3+1 dimensions they are stable only above a minimum amplitude, so that slow radiation carries them below it and they suddenly decay, while in 1 and 2 space dimensions small and moderate ones never decay. Its main limits: a 216-page review built on the author's own D.Sc. thesis, partly his own results; Chapter 2, the introduction and the summary were read, not Chapter 3 on self-gravitating oscillatons, and the derivations were followed in prose, the equations garbled in extraction; apart from the one-parameter family result, the absence of other exact breathers is stated, not derived; and the question whether fine-tuned oscillons are permanent is left against a contrary claim. |
| [LIT-2198](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2198.md) | Decay of Benjamin–Ono solitons under the influence of dissipation | Grimshaw, Smyth & Stepanyants (2018). Adds six kinds of weak loss to the integrable Benjamin–Ono equation and finds, by an energy balance that is the condition for removing secular terms, how its soliton decays: it stays a soliton whose amplitude slides down the family, as A0 e^(−t/τ) under linear (Rayleigh) damping, twice as fast as a linear wave, algebraically, A0/(1 + t/τ)^p, under viscous, Landau, laminar boundary-layer and Chezy losses, and as A0(1 − t/τ), terminally, under radiation into large-scale dispersion. Where the loss does not conserve mass a shelf forms behind the soliton and the adiabatic picture eventually fails; under Landau damping the decaying soliton is exact. Checked against direct numerics. The KdV laws are quoted from earlier work, not derived. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1687](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1687.md)) from the arXiv preprint, v1; worth reading as a compact, numerically checked case of what a weak loss does to an integrable soliton: it does not break up but shrinks along its family of shapes, at a rate fixed by an energy balance, exponentially under linear damping and algebraically under viscous, Landau, boundary-layer and friction losses, and to zero in a finite time under radiation, where in fact it turns into an envelope soliton. Filed as the read neighbour of Kivshar & Malomed (1989), [LIT-2210](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2210.md), for damped solitons. Its limits: one equation, Benjamin–Ono, with the KdV laws quoted from the literature, not derived; no gain or supply; no NLS. |

| [LIT-2200](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2200.md) | Oscillons: Resonant configurations during bubble collapse | Copeland, Gleiser & Müller (1995). Numerical evolution of a spherically symmetric real scalar field in 3+1 dimensions with a symmetric or asymmetric double-well potential. Subcritical bubbles started at rest with Gaussian radius between about 2.4 and 4.5 m^-1 shed part of their energy and enter an "oscillon stage": nearly constant radius (about 2.8–3.0) and energy (about 43 m/λ) whatever the initial radius, almost no radiation for 10^3–10^4 m^-1 against about 5–10 m^-1 in the linear theory, then a quick decay. A Gaussian ansatz explains the minimum radius (R > 2.42, where fluctuations of the core amplitude are unstable), the end (once slow radiation brings the core amplitude below a radius-dependent minimum, the configuration is linear and decays), and which oscillons live longest (the best virialized). No topology or conserved charge protects them. The upper bound on the radius is not explained, and stability was tested only against radial perturbations. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1699](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1699.md)) from arXiv:hep-ph/9503217v2, the first full text, not the version of record; worth reading as the paper that named oscillons and gave the first systematic account of them, and as the record's clearest physical case of a localized structure that persists with no supply, no topological invariant and no conserved charge, holding a near-constant energy for 10^3 to 10^4 m^-1 and then ending abruptly. | [LIT-2204](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2204.md) | Temporal solitons in optical microresonators | Herr, Brasch, Jost, Wang, Kondratiev, Gorodetsky & Kippenberg (2014). A continuous-wave laser swept down in frequency over a resonance of a MgF2 microresonator, from the upper onto the lower branch of its Kerr bistability, produces a series of discrete steps in transmission. Simulations of the coupled-mode (Lugiato-Lefever) equations and the approximate analytic soliton solution identify each step as a state with a definite number of temporal dissipative solitons, about 200 fs pulses on a cw background, fewer at each step; in repeated simulated scans the number varies with the random seeding. The solitons exist only for a normalized detuning between √3 and π²f²/8, have a shape fixed by the resonator and pump, and once formed persist until the pump is switched off; with solitons present the usually unstable red-detuned regime is thermally self-stable. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1692](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1692.md)) from arXiv:1211.0733v3 (27 June 2013), the authors' last arXiv version, not the version of record; worth reading as the first observation of temporal dissipative Kerr solitons in a microresonator and as a clean physical case of a supplied localized structure: held by a continuous pump against cavity loss, existing only in a window of detuning, formed spontaneously from noise during a laser sweep, countable from discrete steps in transmission, and lasting "until the pump laser is switched off". Its main limits: one resonator; simulations without the thermal effects central to the experiment; the existence window from approximate analytics on an infinite domain; path dependence of formation shown, but hysteresis not named and no reverse sweep reported; no decay after switch-off measured; and the run-to-run variation in soliton number reported for simulations only. |
| [LIT-2207](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2207.md) v2 | TASI Lectures on Solitons: Instantons, Monopoles, Vortices and Kinks | Tong (2005). Lectures on instantons, monopoles, vortices and domain walls (kinks), with "Emphasis ... placed on the moduli space of solitons" and their role in supersymmetric gauge theories and string theory. Read here only for topological protection: a configuration of finite energy must approach a vacuum at spatial infinity; maps from infinity into the vacuum manifold fall into homotopy classes, so the space of configurations splits into sectors labelled by a charge measured as a surface term at the boundary; the energy, action or tension in a sector is bounded below by that charge, and the soliton saturates the bound. A kink interpolates between distinct vacua at the two ends, so its charge is fixed by the boundary data. The bounds are saturated in these theories because their couplings are tuned to critical values. Vortex-antivortex pairs are expected to annihilate. | Active — read 2026-11-06 for the topological charge and the kinks ([NOTE-1694](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1694.md)) from arXiv:hep-th/0509216v5, as a neighbour of Copeland, Gleiser & Müller (1995), [LIT-2200](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2200.md), for the topological protection that oscillons lack; worth reading as a standard statement of why a topological soliton persists: a finite-energy configuration must reach a vacuum at infinity, the map from infinity into the vacua falls into homotopy classes that cannot be deformed into one another, and the class is a charge, measured at the boundary, that bounds the energy from below. Its main limits for this record: lectures on supersymmetric gauge theories and BPS solitons, not a plain introduction to kinks, with no worked φ4 kink; annihilation is assumed, for vortices only; and the thesis that such solitons can end only by annihilation or at a boundary is the reader's inference, not Tong's sentence. Read for the topological charge and the kinks: §1.1, §2.1, §§3.1–3.2, §3.8.3, §§4.1–4.3.2; the moduli spaces, constructions and applications not read. |
| [LIT-2208](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2208.md) | Soliton | Zabusky & Porter (2010). An encyclopedia article on solitons by Zabusky, co-author of the 1965 letter that named them. A solitary wave is a localized wave of translation held by a balance of nonlinear and dispersive effects; a soliton is one that keeps its shape at constant speed and emerges from a collision with another unchanged except possibly for a phase shift. It traces the history from Russell's 1834 observation through Korteweg and de Vries, Zabusky and Kruskal's 1965 numerical KdV solutions, and the inverse scattering method, and lists the relatives: topological solitons, kinks, dissipative solitons, oscillons and others, which in general lack the soliton's interaction properties. | Active — read in full 2026-11-06 ([NOTE-1689](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1689.md)) from the article page at scholarpedia.org; worth reading as the shortest authoritative account of what a soliton is, by the co-author of the paper that named it: a solitary wave held by a balance of nonlinearity and dispersion, which keeps its shape and comes out of a collision with another unchanged except for a phase shift, with the history from Russell through Zabusky and Kruskal to inverse scattering and a catalogue of relatives (topological, dissipative, oscillons). Filed as the read neighbour of Zabusky & Kruskal (1965), [LIT-2199](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2199.md), and in part of Kivshar & Malomed (1989), [LIT-2210](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2210.md). Its limits: an encyclopedia article; the relatives are named, not treated, so it gives nothing on thresholds, hysteresis or topological protection. |
