A review of ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction (VIDD): in animals a few hours of fully controlled ventilation lower diaphragm force, with atrophy from less synthesis and more proteolysis driven by oxidative stress; in humans, biopsies from brain-dead donors (Levine 2008 and its follow-up, Hussain 2010, the authors' own study) show the same atrophy, injury and proteolytic markers, correlated with ventilation's duration, while the pectoralis is unchanged, and twitch tracheal pressure fell by 32% over six days. Keeping spontaneous effort lessens VIDD in animals but leaves a residual deficit. The earlier doctrine of "diaphragmatic rest" is reversed. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1702.md)) from the open-access full text in Europe PMC (PMC3219309); worth reading as a compact account, by authors of one of the biopsy studies, of how fully controlled mechanical ventilation weakens, shrinks and injures the human diaphragm within days, and as the stand-in for the unread Levine et al. (2008). Its limits: a narrative review; the human evidence is small case-control biopsy series in brain-dead donors and observational twitch-pressure studies, with confounding by sedation and illness conceded; the evidence that partial support protects is from animals; recovery after ventilation is unstudied. |

Here it is the physiological case of support that does all of a capacity's work removing that capacity within days. | Unavailable — not read; no lawful full text reached as of 2026-11-05. The report of an international consensus conference of April 2005, an 11-member jury answering five questions on weaning, defined as "the entire process of liberating the patient from mechanical support and from the endotracheal tube". | [LIT-2214](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2214.md) | Adrenal Insufficiency in Corticosteroids Use: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis | Broersen, Pereira, Jørgensen & Dekkers (2015). A systematic review and meta-analysis of 74 articles (3,753 adult corticosteroid users, 1975–2014) estimating how many are biochemically adrenal-insufficient, their own cortisol production suppressed. The pooled share runs from 4.2% after nasal use to 48.7% after oral and 52.2% after intra-articular use; in asthma it rises with dose (2.4%, 8.5%, 21.5%) and duration (1.4% under a month, 27.4% over a year). On retesting after stopping it falls from 38.7% to 14.9% at 4 weeks after short high-dose courses and from 56.4% to 25.3% at 6 months after long medium-dose use. The authors find no route, dose, duration or disease at which the risk can be excluded, and note that no withdrawal scheme has been shown efficient or safe. | Active — read 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1703](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1703.md)) from the reprint that is chapter 2 of Broersen's 2019 Leiden PhD thesis (hdl 1887/78950, Open Access); the supplements were not read; worth reading as the quantitative case of an outside supply of a hormone leaving the body's own production of it suppressed after the supply stops, with gradients by route, dose and duration. Pooling 74 observational articles, it finds suppression in 4.2% after nasal use up to 52.2% after intra-articular use, rising in asthma with dose (2.4% to 21.5%) and duration (1.4% to 27.4%), and receding incompletely after stopping (to 14.9% at 4 weeks and 25.3% at 6 months). High risk of bias, no individual-patient data, route, dose, duration and disease not disentangled; the two retest groups differ in regimen and interval together, so they cannot show that longer use means longer recovery; Figure 4 mislabels the 6-month retest as after 4 weeks; no taper data. |

Ventilation can be stopped abruptly in about 75% of patients whose cause of respiratory failure has improved; readiness is tested by a trial of unassisted breathing on T-tube or pressure support of 7 cmH2O, 30 and 120 min being equivalent, and immediate extubation after a passed trial shortens ventilation compared with gradual withdrawal. For the quarter who fail, gradual withdrawal while causes are corrected: in Brochard's trial pressure support was shortest, in Esteban's once-daily T-tube trials were best, and in both SIMV did worst. Resting fatigued muscles with ventilation is held to be the only treatment of fatigue. The abstract states the reverse on SIMV. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1701](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1701.md)) from the open-access full text in Europe PMC (PMC137330); worth reading as a summary, by the lead of one of the trials, of the randomized evidence on how to withdraw ventilation: abrupt withdrawal after a passed trial for most patients, gradual withdrawal for those who fail. Its limits: a narrative review by an interested trialist, of trials now about thirty years old; its abstract says SIMV is the most effective method of weaning after failed trials while its body says, twice, that it is the least; a correction published in 2006 (doi:10.1186/cc4996) was not read, and that it fixes the abstract is unverified. |

| [LIT-2217](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2217.md) | Prolonged weaning from mechanical ventilation: who, what, when and how? | Shah, Hart & Kaltsakas (2024). Weaning runs in four steps: treat the cause, assess readiness daily, test the response to reduced support with a spontaneous breathing trial of at least 30 min, then extubate. Patients are grouped as simple (weaned at the first attempt), difficult (up to three trials or seven days) or prolonged (more), following the 2007 consensus. Predictors of readiness have low power and clinicians underestimate readiness; delay harms. Prolonged weaning is a load-capacity-drive imbalance managed by a team; about half of those who fail weaning remain on invasive ventilation at one year. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1706](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1706.md)) from the open-access full text in Europe PMC (PMC11629167, CC BY-NC 4.0); worth reading as a current account of how weaning is tested and classified, restating the 2007 consensus' three groups and definition of failure, and for how badly prolonged weaning ends. Anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid doses invariably suppress the HPA axis by negative feedback, and prolonged use brings pituitary hyporesponsiveness and adrenal atrophy. Courses under 3–4 weeks can be stopped without taper; longer ones are tapered once the disease is controlled, fast at high doses and slowly near the physiologic dose, with replacement low enough to leave a stimulus for recovery, and recovery is checked by morning cortisol read as a continuum.
